总序
随着《国家中长期教育改革和发展规划纲要（2010-2020年）》的颁发，我
国高等教育吹响了全面深化教学改革的号角，“人才培养在高校工作中钓中心地
位”得以正式确立。教育部即将颁布高等学校各类专业本科教学质量《国家标准》，
第一次以国家标准的形式对本科教学质量提出刚性要求。在此背景下，全国高校
英语类专业本科教学改革正围绕人才培养这一中心任务全面展开。
一、英语类专业向何处去？
随着教学改革和教学研究的深入推进，国内英语教育界对英语类专业的发展
方向逐步形成共识。就学科定位而言，英语类专业应加强学科本位建设和人文通
识教育；就培养目标而言，应根据国家经济和社会发展需要以及各级各类高校的
差异定位和学生个性化发展的需求，培养不同层次、不同类型的多元化外语人才；
就培养模式而言，应在明确和巩固本专业学科内涵的基础上，通过与校内其他学
科之间的复合以及国内外联合培养，为学生的专业学习奠定坚实的学科基础，开
辟广阔的发展空间；就培养规格而言，应重视在语言、文学和文化核心专业知识
基础上为学生搭建跨学科的知识结构，突出对思辨能力和跨文化能力的培养；
就课程设置而言，应适当压缩英语技能课程课时，用“内容依托”或“内容与语
言融合”的教学理念改造和加强传统英语技能课程，同时系统建设语言学、文
学、跨文化研究、国别与区域研究以及相关专业方向课程。
可见，经过多年的探索，英语界在英语类专业的学科定位、培养目标、培养
模式、培养规格和课程设置等宏观问题上已明确发展思路，为下一轮教学改革指
明了前进方向。
二、英语教育如何升级？
与高校其他专业相比，英语类专业在课程设置上具有一个显著的特点，这就是，
该专业70%左右的专业课时均投入语言技能的训练，所导致的问题是专业知识课
程受到严重挤压。因此，面向未来，英语类专业全面深化本科教学改革所面临的
首要挑战就是要在重新认识英语教育规律的基础上，全面深化对语言技能课程
改革。
经过近10年的教改实践和理论探索，我们得出的基本结论是：
。 英语教育本质上属于人文教育，必须在语言学习的全过程中促进学生人文
素养的提高。人文素养是指：文学、历史、哲学、艺术、宗教和社会学等领
Writing Critically 1
域人文知识；爱人类、爱真理、爱文化、爱自然人文精神；博学、审问、
慎思、明辨、笃行的人文品格。
• 英语教育应克服“思辨缺席症”，致力于全方位培养学生的思辨能力，包
括认知技能和情感态度，为学生的学术深造、创新创业和终身发展奠基。
• 技能课程知识化（技能课程的材料必须系统呈现外语学科人文基础知
识），知识课程技能化（知识课程必须同时促进学生语言能力的持续发展），
以及技能课程思辨化，知识课程思辨化，此“四化”为英语专业培养学生思
辨能力的根本途径。
• 英语专业技能课程思辨化有赖于：为思辨设定标准（教学目标）；为忠辨
提供原料（教学内容）；为思辨搭建工作坊（教学活动）；为思辨培养教师（教
学主导）。
。 进入高校英语类专业学习阶段，语言学习应由显入隐，知识学习则由隐入
显，实现以内容为依托或语言与内容融合的英语教学。
• 英语教育应促进学生跨文化能力的全面提升，后者是全球化时代英语专业
人才的核心竞争力。
。 思辨能力可以通过对跨文化问题的探究得到提升，跨文化能力则可以通过
对思辨能力的运用得到提升，两者相互促进，相得益彰。
• 思辨的前提是自主学习，思辨能力可以通过自主学习来增养，开最终促进
自主学习能力的提高。
三、《大学思辨英语教程》的使命
基于上述教育和教学理念，我们在总结近10年教学改革实践经验的基础上组
织编写了《大学思辨英语教程》。本系列教程致力于全面对接《高等学校外国语
言文学类专业本科教学质量国家标准》所规定的人才培养的素质、知识和能力指
标，特别是人文素养、学科知识、语言能力、思辨能力、跨文化能力和自主学习
能力，旨在为高等学校英语类专业提供基础阶段听、说、读、写课程教学全面
解决方案。
顾名思义，“思辨”构成了本系列教程的鲜明特点。我们倡导通过思辨来学习
英语，通过英语来学习思辨，将思辨一以贯之，融合英语教育与人文教育，实现
语言能力、人文素养、学科知识、思辨能力、跨文化能力和自主学习能力的相互
促进，同步提升。我们坚信，高校英语类专业钓语言教学应该而且能够超越传统
的语言基本功训练，从英语教学走向英语教育，赋予学生在知识爆炸和全球化时代
获取信息、探索真知、参与社会建设、跨越文化屏障和创造美好生活的思辨能力。
四、走向思辨
英语教育与思辨能力培养并提，并非因为思辨能力培养是英语教育的独特属
性。事实上，思辨能力培养乃是整个高等教育的终极目标之一。哈佛大学以培养
学生“乐于发现和思辨”（rejoice in discovery and in critical thought）为宗旨；剑
桥大学也把“鼓励怀疑精神” （the encouragement of a questioning spirit）纳入大学
使命。美国学者彼得•法乔恩（Peter Facione）一言以蔽之，“教育，不折不扣，
就是学会思考。”
《礼记•中庸》日：“博学之，审问之，慎思之，明辨之，笃行之。”中国
古代圣贤们一直以“思辨”为座右铭。《中华人民共和国高等教育法》规定：“高
等教育的任务是培养具有创新精神和实践能力的高级专门人才。”而创新精神和
实践能力的根本依托正是思辨能力。
显然，思辨能力培养乃是高等教育一个永恒命题，在当下中国高等教育以
内涵式发展、质量提升和创新能力培养为导向的新一轮教育改革中，其重要件更
加凸显。而对于中国高等英语教育的深化改革而言，思辨能力培养就尤为紧迫了。
我们的英语教育与思辨能力培养还存在很大差距。英语教育，尤其是基础阶段语
言教学，往往专注于语言技能的打磨，不重视学科训练和人文通识教育，因而大
量的教学活动都是在模仿、理解和识记层面展开，很少上升到应用、分析、评价
和创造高级思维层次。英语教育往往把语言的习得和知识的获取隔离开来，人
为划分了基础阶段语言学习和高级阶段知识学习两个区间，因而常常忽略了在四
年本科教育过程中一以贯之地帮助学生通过语言获取知识，同时在获取知识的过
程中夯实语言，提高思辨能力。此种状况延续多年，现已危及英语教育生存与
发展。面向未来，英语教育无疑必须继承“基本功”教学的优良传统，但同时要
积极创新，超越传统，在思辨能力培养上实现根本突破。
西方学术界对思辨能力进行了大量的研究。美国哲学界发布的《德尔菲报告》
（The Delphi Report,1990）对思辨能力提出了一个颇具权威性的定义：
我们把思辨能力理解为有目的的、自我调节的判断，它建立在对证据、
概念、方法、标准或背景等因素的阐述、分析、评价、推理与解释之上。
思辨能力是至关重要的探究工具。因此，思辦能力在教育中是一种解放力量，
在个人和公民生活中是一种强大的资源。尽管它并不等同于完善思维（good
thinking），思辨能力是一种普遍的自我矫正的人类现象。一个具有思辦能
力的理想的思考者习惯于勤学好问、博闻多识、相信理性、心胸开阔、灵
活应变、在做出评价时保持公正、在面对个人偏见时保持诚实、在做出判
断时保持谨慎、愿意重新考虑、面对问题头脑清晰、处理复杂事务井井有条、
勤于搜寻相关信息、选择标准时理由充分、探究问题时专注目标、持之以
恒地追求所探索的问题与研究条件许可的尽可能精确的结果。因此，培养
具有思辨能力的思考者就意味着为此理想而奋斗。它把思辨能力的开发与
上述品质的培养结合起来，由此不断产出有用的真知灼见，这也正是一个
理性和民主社会白基础。
高校英语类专业教育如果要承担起作为大学教育崇高使命，就必须积极迎
接思辨能力培养所提出的全面挑战。由于英语专业技能课程占据了英语专业一半
以上的课时，这就意味着英语专业技能课程能否有效培养学生的思辨能力将直接
Writing Critically 1
关系到整个英语专业的兴衰成败。
当前，在《高等学校外国语言文学类专业本科教学质量国家标准》的指导下，
英语类专业新一轮的教学改革正如火如茶地展开。我们诚挚希望《大学思辨英语
教程》的出版，为传统语言教学插上思辨与跨文化的翅膀，为英语教育的健康快
速发展注入强劲动力，为英语类专业人才培养的全面升级提供坚实支撑！

VI Writing Critically 1
二、使用对象
本系列教程可供高等学校英语类专业（英语语言文学、翻译、商务英语）本
科基础阶段（一、二年级）四个学期使用。各高校可根据学生和师资特点，在课
时和学期分布上适当灵活安排。
本教程也可供高校非英语专业高年级或非英语专业研究生使用。当前，一些
高校纷纷推出形式多样的创新人才培养项目，重视培养学生的高层次学术英语、
人文素养、思辨能力和跨文化能力，提倡全英文教学，本教程是此类项目的理想
选择。
三、主要特点
本系列教程致力于在英语技能课程教学中全面贯彻落实《高等学校外国语言
文学类专业本科教学质量国家标准》的外语教育理念与人才培养规格，具有如下
主要特点：
1.主题引领听说读写，牢固搭建人文知识结构
与传统基础英语教材不同的是，《大学思辨英语教程》听说读写四大分系列
均按知识逻辑和主题单元系统展开。分系列内部各分册知识内容均涉及人文社会
科学一个统一的知识领域，各单元按主题依次推进，探讨该知识领域的经典和
重要话题；而各分系列的平行各分册之间则进一步在内容上相互呼应，彼此补充。
换言之，本系列教程不仅是语言教程，而且是知识教程，旨在帮助学生运用英语
比较系统地学习语言、文化、文学、历史、哲学乃至社会学领域的学科知识，搭
建跨学科的知识结构，提高人文素养，为进入高年级学习本专业或相关专业的知
识课程奠定坚实学科基础。
2.精细夯实语言功底，全面拓展学术英语能力
英语专业基础阶段听说读写教材毫无疑问要为学生打下坚实的英语“基本功”。
为此，《大学思辨英语教程》继承了北京外国语大学英语专业精细训练听说读写
的优良传统，并大胆探索非母语环境下英语学习的新路径。精读分系列各单元设
有语言进阶（Language Enhancement）部分，从词、句、段、篇，到修辞和文体，
通过形式多样、行之有效练习形式，巩固和提高学生各项英语技能；写作分
系列对记叙文、说明文、议论文和学术论文等不同文体的写作循序展开扎实训练，
并将英语学科的相关定量与定性基本研究方法纳入课程内容；口语分系列由易入
难，引导学生运用英语从交际到讨论到演讲到辩论，循序渐进；听力分系列基于
国内外听力研究的最新成果，以听力策略训练为突破口，融合视、听、读、写、说，
全面提高各种情景特别是学术情景下通过听力准确获取并批判性评价信息的能力。
与传统的基础英语教材相比，本系列教程重视引导学生登堂入室，进入学术英语
领地，运用英语就人文社会科学领域的学术话题进行富有挑战性的输入和输出活
动，全面拓展学术英语能力。
前言
3.严格遵循思维规律，系统训练思辨创新能力
学术界对思辨能力构成要素及其发展规律已进行了大量的研究，为本系列教
程听说读写练习活动的设计提供了坚实理论基础。例如，美国哲学界发布的《德
尔菲报告》提出的“专家共识”；保罗等学者（Paul, Binker, Jensen & Kreklau）
提出35层级思辨能力指标体系；本杰明•布鲁姆 （Benjamin Bloom）和洛杯・安
德森（Lorin Anderson）提出的认知分层理论。在对课文的阅读练习设计中，我
们重点参考了理查德•保罗和琳达•埃尔德（Richard Paul & Linda Elder）提出
的思辨理论框架和训练模型。根据这一理论，思辨性文本均包括8项“思维要
素”（Elements of Thought），即：目的 （purposes），问题（questions），视角
（points of view），信息（information），推理（inferences），概念（concepts），
假设（assumptions），影响（implications）。思辨能力训练就是运用“普遍思辨
标准” （Universal Intellectual Standards）系统拷问上述思维要素，这套标准包括10
项指标：清晰性（clarity），准确性（accuracy），精确性（precision），相夫性
（relevance），深刻性（depth），广阔性（breadth），完整性（completeness），
逻辑性（logic），重要性（significance），公正性（faimess）。经过这样系统的
训练，学习者最终养成8项思辨品质：谦虚（intellectual humility），独立（intellectual
autonomy），诚实（intellectual integrity），勇气 （intellectual courage），毅力
（intellectual perseverance），相信理性 （confidence in reason），同理心（intellectual
empathy），公正心（fairmindedness）。思辨能力培养的最终目标就是要使良好的
思维习惯成为学生的“第二本能”。基于上述理念，本系列教程听说读写各分系
列均把思辨能力各项认知技能和品质技能纳入各单元核心教学目标，设计了多样
化的相关练习和任务，有针对性地进行系统训练，将思辨能力培养落到实处，坚
持到底。
4.一以贯之中外比较，全方位提升跨文化能力

编写说明
学习写作通常是从记叙文写作开始的，因为记叙文写作最贴近我们的生活。
简而言之，记叙文写作就是“写故事”，用文字记录发生在自己身边的故事或
听到的故事。《写作1：记叙文写作》将帮助学习者学会赏析记叙文佳作，掌
握记叙文写作的核心技巧，激活已有的中文记叙文写作经验，盘活已学过英
文词汇及语法知识，并学习敏锐地观察生活、思考人生，最终学会用英文生动
地讲述故事。
本册写作教程基于如下编写原则：
1.读写结合，相互促进。阅读是内容和技巧的输人，写作则是内容和技巧的输出，
两者相互依赖，相得益彰。
2. 写作活动是学生独立与合作进行探索的过程，是一个知识建构、思维训练
和精神成长的过程。在英语教育的大背景下，写作课程应该而且能够有效
促进学生的人文教育，提高思辨能力和跨文化能力。
3.写作不是一次性活动，而是过程性活动。写作任务设计应该让学生反复
体验选题、构思、搜集素材、创作、修改等写作活动的全过程。写作教学
的最终目标是培养独立的作者。
4.同伴评估是写作教学的有效方法。通过对习作的同伴评估，学习者建立学
习共同体，运用作文评价标准，相互批评和鼓励，既有利于打开写作思路，
相互改进，相互学习，也有利于不断内化所学的写作技巧。
5.写作教学和其他课程教学一样，应重视学生自主学习能力的提升。因此，
教材应为学习者设计可供自主阅读的深人浅出的写作知识，可供独立欣赏
和借鉴丰富多彩的示例和范文，可供独立完成或小组探索的活动设计以
及可供自我检测的学习目标和评价标准。
基于上述编写原则，本册写作教程凸显如下特点：
1） 循序渐进，专项训练写作技巧
每单元围绕一个写作技巧专题展开。第一单元对记叙文写作进行了概述。
随后第二至第八单元针对记叙文写作的核心要素逐一阐释，包括人物刻画、
场景描写、叙述视角、主题设定、情节展开、写作风格和意象使用。为了帮助
学习者更好地理解记叙文写作技巧，每个单元都提供了名篇案例解析，并配以
X Writing Critically 1
相应的练习，以分析现固所学的写作技巧。建议学生课前自学这部分内容，教
师在课堂上组织和引导学生分享他们的理解，并对有歧义的内容进行重点讲解
和讨论。
2）主题导引，培养思辨能力和跨文化能力
每单元根据主题配有两篇名家名作，供课上作为范文进行分析和讨论。
主题包括： Life and Value, Empathy and Justice, Growth and Maturity, Truth and
Interpretation, Dream and Faith, Conflict and Harmony, Ethnicity and Identity, Love
and Eternity。通过思考和讨论这些具有永恒意义的人文主题，学生不仅可以观
摩写作技巧，打开思路，获得写作选题的灵感，而且能够反思社会和人生，提
高人文素养，培养思辨能力和跨文化能力。
3）练习形式灵活多样，让学习充满挑战和惊喜
每单元的写作练习形式包括小作业“活动”（Activity），大作业“习作”
（Assignment）和学期“创作”（Term Project）。每个小作业是为完成大作业
进行铺垫。针对记叙文的写作特点，本教程所设计的学期创作作业旨在帮助学
生整合每单元所学的记叙文写作技巧，在各单元学习过程中逐步完成一篇创作
性记叙文作品，从而在文学创作层次上体会记叙文写作技巧，享受创作的乐趣，
培养创新能力。
4） 明确设定学习目标，让学生自主驾驭学习过程
每单元开头提出了明确的学习目标，与该单元结尾处的自我评价清单遥相
呼应。学习者在每单元学习结束后，对照学习目标进行自我评价。此外，本教
程附录中还提供了“习作自评表”，供学生在课内外对习作进行同伴评估和独
立评估时使用。日积月累，潜移默化，优秀作文的标准将逐步内化为学生的写
作习惯，进而形成独立写作的能力。
5）语言训练细致人微，不断夯实基本功
每单元设计了 Language Study 部分，针对记叙文写作的语言特点，对选词、
句子结构、时间顺序、时态、各类修辞手段等进行系统训练。该部分的讲解和
练习与各单元的范文案例分析相配合，引导学生观摩和实践记叙文写作的语言
策略，不断夯实语言基础，提高语言的准确性和感染力。
本册教程共设计八个单元，每个单元的教学约需要四个学时，供大学一年级
或二年级学生使用。

Unit 1 Life and Value
Part I: Learning the Skills
• What is narrative?
"Narrative' is another word for "story.' Narrative writing shows the writer's
ideas in a creative way. The story may be a realistic account with true events and real
people-known as non-fiction. Or it may have made-up characters or events that
are not real-called fiction. The type of narrative you choose to write depends on the
story that you have to tell and the way you want to tell it.
Narrative writing is a major literary genre, with lots of "mini-genres" within it.
Here are a few of them:
In adventures, the characters must face challenges, often life-threatening, and
overcome obstacles in their way.
Animal stories are about animals. The characters may be realistic, or they may
act and speak like humans.
Biographies tell the true story of a person's life. They share facts about the
subject's personality, struggles and accomplishments. Autobiography is the story of a
person's life narrated by himself or herself.
Fantasies are about extraordinary experiences that do not usually happen in real
life. They may include creatures, places, events and inventions that exist only in the
author's imagination.
Folklore is traditional stories handed down from generation to generation. It
contains memorable characters (animal or human). Fables are like folklore, but a
fable usually teaches a lesson.
Historical narratives tell stories that took place in the past. They may be real or
imagined stories, but they are based on people, places or events that once existed.
Humorous narratives are funny. They may also have serious parts, but the main
goal is to make the reader laugh through the amusing personalities, conflicts and
actions of the characters.
Multicultural narratives focus on a different culture or ethnic group. They tell
about people and places that may not be familiar to every reader.
Mysteries have a puzzle or secret that needs to be discovered or explained. The
main character(s) usually attempt(s) to gather clues that will "unlock" the mystery.
Realistic narratives are about people, places and events that could be true. The
story is believable and actually could happen.
Romances spotlight love and relationships, but the "road to happiness' is usually
bumpy.
Science fiction uses ideas from science and technology to create stories,
sometimes on other planets.
Writing Critically 1
Which genre(s) have you read? Which interests you most? Writers usually
choose to write narratives in the genre or genres they find enjoyable.
Read Example 1 and consider:
• Which mini-genre of narrative writing does it belong to?
• What facts are presented?
• What writing techniques can you identify?
• Do these writing techniques affect your response to the wolf?
Example 1
Walk with a wolf in the cold air before sunrise. She moves, quiet as mist, between
spruce trees and birches. A silent grey shadow, she slides between boulders and trots
over blue pebbles to the edge of the lake. She plunges through slush ice and laps the chill
water, snaps at a feather that drifts down from a goose wing, then splashes to shore and
shakes herself like a dog. There's deep snow on the mountains. Snow clouds bank in the
east. Winter is coming, and the geese fly south.
-Walk with a Wolf by Janni Howker
Walk with a Wolf is written to challenge what the author perceives to be the
unfair stereotypical representation of the wolf in traditional stories. It takes the reader
on a journey with the wolves of the Yukon Territory in Canada. It is a realistic animal
story. In this passage, we can gather the following factual information:
• Wolves are active in the early morning.
• They live in forested areas.
• There are icy cold lakes in the Yukon Territory.
• The wolf behaves in a manner similar to a dog.
• Geese leave the Yukon Territory when winter comes.
To "walk" with the wolf is to share a day in its life-a day that begins with a
visit to the lake to drink water. The last sentence "Winter is coming, and the geese
fly south" prepares the reader for the next stage in the story; at this point we might
infer that the wolf does not travel south with the geese. We are being encouraged to
anticipate as Howker builds suspense. We ask ourselves: "What will the wolf do when
winter comes?ại
Howker uses descriptive language to illustrate the actions of the wolf in the
early morning and the environment where it lives, including verbs such as move,
slide, plunge, snap, splash and shake, and adjectives such as cold, quiet, silent, grey,
blue, chill and deep. Howker's poetic prose elicits feelings of wonder and respect; the
reader is invited to admire the wolf's agility and stealth, its ability to move "quiet
as mist." It stimulates an emotional response. The wolf's behavior mirrors that of a
playful domestic animal as it "snaps at a feather" in the way a pet might snap at a
thrown ball. The image of it shaking water from its coat brings to view a pet dog that
has plunged into a pond to chase a stick. The similarity is further emphasized by the
direct comparison "like a dog."

• What are the elements of narrative writing?
All narratives have a beginning, middle and ending. The beginning is
important. It must be interesting enough to capture the reader' attention so that they
want to read more. The beginning introduces the subject of the narrative and sets the
mood and direction. The middle is called the main body. This section is the biggest
one. It contains the ideas, facts and events that make up most of the story. The ending
wraps up the story. It can satisfy the reader by solving a problem or answering a
question.
Narratives contain story elements such as character(s), setting, plot, point of
view and theme. Characters are animated beings with emotions, motivations and
intention. They move in the time and space of a story, interacting with friends and
foes, reflecting and taking action. The character is often the most important element
because the experience the author creates for readers is centered on a character or
group of characters. Usually, the main character(s) is(are) fully developed, but the
supporting characters are portrayed much less vividly than the main character(s).
The extent to which the supporting characters are developed depends on the author's
purpose and the needs of the story. Authors must determine how to develop and
present characters to involve readers in the experiences they are writing about. They
develop characters in four ways: through appearance, action, dialogue and monologue.
Setting includes the main features in terms of time, place and situation. These
features are not to be memorized and recited, but to be explored to understand
the general mood of the story and feelings of the characters. In some stories, the
Unit 1 Life and Value
setting is barely sketched, which is called a backdrop setting. For example, in many
folktales, the setting is relatively unimportant, and the convention "Once upon
a time.." can be used to set the scene. In other stories, however, the setting is
elaborate and is integral to the story's effectiveness; these are called integral settings.
Some stories could take place anywhere, and the setting requires little description;
others, however, require a specific setting, and authors must take care to ensure
the authenticity of the historical period or geographic location in which the story
is set.
Plot is the sequence of events involving characters in conflict situations in the
beginning, middle and ending of a story. The plot is based on the goals of one or
more characters. For example, the main character(s) may want to achieve a certain
goal, and other characters may try to prevent the main characters) from achieving
that goal or help the main character(s) along the way. The story is thus put in
motion.
Through choices in points of view, the author decides what the reader will see
and know. The view can be limited to the actions of characters or spread to their
innermost thoughts and feelings. The view can offer insight into a single character
or expand to everyone involved in the story. Point of view is the outlook on the
action that the reader will follow. In the objective point of view, the action speaks for
itself. The innermost feelings of characters are not revealed, and readers must infer
intention and motivation only from what characters say and do. In the first person
point of view,I is both the character and the narrator, speaking as an eyewitness
and a participant in the events. In the omniscient point of view, the author is godlike,
seeing and knowing all. The author tells the reader about the thought processes of
each character without worrying about how the information is obtained.
Theme is the underlying meaning of a story and embodies general truths about
society or human nature. The theme usually deals with the characters' emotions
and values. Themes can be stated explicitly or implicitly. Explicit themes are stated
openly and clearly in the story, whereas implicit themes are suggested through the
characters' actions, dialogue and monologue as they strive to resolve their problems.
In Example 3 on Pages 5 and 6, there are two main characters: Hare and Tortoise.
It takes the omniscient point of view to tell the reader what the characters think and
do in the story. The setting is not explicitly indicated, similar to other fairy tales. The
plot starts with the bet between Hare and Tortoise about a race of speed and moves
through three stages of the race. In the first stage of the race, Hare took the lead
and Tortoise kept on moving. In the second stage of the race, Hare took a nap and
Tortoise kept on moving. At last, Hare woke up too late, and Tortoise won the race.
The theme of the story is explicitly conveyed through Tortoise's words, "slow and
steady wins every time!"

to reveal all things to me, and, more than all things else, to love me.

had dressed it; but I did not know this until afterward. When I had played with it

know that I was spelling a word or even that words existed; I was simply making my

uncomprehending way a great many words, among them pin, hat, cup and a few

• Time expressions
Before doing narrative writing, it helps to organize the events you have thought
about by using a timeline, preparing for your later selection of the events to be
included in your writing. For example, if we want to write about Helen Keller, we can
organize the key events in the life of Helen Keller as follows:
1. On June 27, 1880, Helen Keller was born in Tuscumbia, Alabama. When she was
19 months old, Helen had a severe illness that caused her to become blind and
deaf.
2. In 1887 Anne Sullivan became Helen's teacher. Anne taught Helen how to
communicate. Over time, Helen learned to speak and read braille, as well as write.
3. In 1900 Helen was accepted to Radcliffe College. She graduated in 1904.
4. In 1903 Helen published her first book The Story of My Life.
5. In 1915 Helen founded Helen Keller International, a non-profit organization that
helped make life better for blind people all over the world. She began to travel to
give lectures about ways to prevent visual blindness.
6. In 1964 Helen was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom for her
contribution to society.

• Concrete details
Details are the lifeblood of good writing-for both fictional and non-fictional
narrative. It is not just any details, but concrete details, or details that are grounded
in the five senses. By first and foremost relying on what we see, feel, hear, touch and
taste when we render out thoughts and emotions on the page, we are ensuring that
we immerse our readers in a concrete sensory world of our own making. You won't
see the forest unless you see this tree and that tree and that tree, that is, unless you
focus on the details with great specificity. In other words, you can start off your
writing from smallness and specificity-eschewing grand ideas in favor of thinking
particularly. Furthermore, it is important to be selective. You have to choose your
trees if you want your readers to be interested. Making choices-and rendering them
precisely-is at the heart of all good writing.
Some Definitions
Specific: Limiting or limited. Precise. Peculiar to, or characteristic of, something.
Exclusive or special.
Concrete: Characterized by things or events that can be perceived by the senses.
Real. Referring to a particular entity. The reproduction, using descriptions embodying
the five senses, of a place, person or thing.
General: Emphasizing the general character rather than the specific details of
something, making it vague or indefinite.
Abstract: Dissociated from any specific instance. Expressing a quality apart from
an object. The reverse of a concrete detail.

Part I: Learning the Skills
• What are characters?
Characters are central to narrative writing. We want to create real characters:
characters that live and breathe and act in believable ways, and most importantly,
characters whom our readers will find worth caring about. Just like real creatures,
characters have strengths and weaknesses, and they have specific personalities.
The main character in a narrative is known as the protagonist. There may be one
or more main characters. The other characters are called secondary characters. They
may help the protagonist or get in his or her way.
In a fictional narrative, the characters are made up but can be based on real people.
Some narratives, such as science fiction and fantasy, use animals or imaginary creatures
as characters. In contrast, the characters in non-fictional narratives are real. They may be
alive or dead, but at one time they did exist.
Think about your favorite characters in those narratives you have enjoyed. What
do they look like? What are their personalities? What are their likes and dislikes? The
way to create memorable characters is to get to know them and to write about them
as if they were real.
• How to develop characters?
Before learning how to develop characters, we first need to know the differences
between flat and round characters. Flat characters are also called stereotypes, and
the hallmark of flat characters is that they are incapable of surprising us; they act in
a prescribed way, and are utterly consistent, without complexity. For example, the
loving mother, the evil stepfather, the cruel boss and the happy kid are all examples
of flat characters that lack the complexity and emotional depth of the real people we
know. A round character is the opposite: He or she is capable of surprising us-with
unexpected fits of anger or an uplifting sense of humor or a snide remark about a
presumed friend. But "surprising" doesn't mean "unbelievable." Although surprising,
it is still possible for the character to do that. As E. M. Forster, a British writer, says,
if a character never surprises us, then he or she is flat; if they surprise but do not
convince us, they are only flat pretending to be round.
Characters are introduced and developed through a range of techniques and
conventions. Here are some common ways:
1. What the character looks like
This is one of the most basic ways of introducing and defining a character:
through the description of his or her physical characteristics using straight narrative.
This method can also include descriptions of a character's environment and

without some degree of narrative description of this type.

of his head, and he looked as if he had just come from a concert.

• How to craft effective dialogue?
Dialogue is the conversation between characters. It should sound natural, as
if the characters were really speaking. Learning to craft good dialogue is one of the
Unit 2 Empathy and Justice
most critical aspects of learning to write good fictional and non-fictional narrative.
Dialogue is not just the words the characters speak to each other. Good dialogue
works on a number of different levels. Here are the main aspects that should be
accomplished with it:
• to add to the reader's knowledge of the situation.
• to move forward the action of the plot.
• to reveal something about the speaker's personality, both directly and indirectly.
• to dramatize relationships between characters.
• to build suspense.
When you write dialogue, it is important to stay true to each character's
personality and background. Dialogue should be extremely specific. Every character
should speak differently. Each should have a distinct way of phrasing opinion and
subject matter. You should consider:
The character's age. How old the character is helps determine what words he or
she will use.
Where he or she lives. People from different areas have different ways of
speaking.
Where he or she is speaking. A character will speak differently in different
places.
Whom he or she is talking to. A character will use different words when he or
she is talking to different people.
Form of communication. A person may use different styles of language when
speaking from those he or she uses in writing.
The character's mood. How the character feels is often expressed through dialogue.
For example, when a person is angry, he or she might say things harsher than usual.

• Gestures are a part of dialogue.
• Silence is a part of dialogue.
• The environment (the scene around the character) can also be a part of dialogue.
• Dialogue is not necessarily grammatically correct.

"I've never seen one," he was dismissing what the girl said. When the girl looked at
the bead curtain, she was trying to change the subject to defuse the tension between
them. In both cases, the gestures can be considered extensions of the dialogue.
In general, having your characters do something while they are speaking adds
verisimilitude to the exchange; we rarely just sit there, frozen, as we speak to one
another. It is natural for gestures and actions to enter into the dialogue itself.
• Balance telling and showing in narrative writing
It is important to balance the acts of telling and showing in developing
characters. Ideally, showing and telling are organically intertwined. However, a
common practice is "to show, not tell.' This is because good telling is difficult to do.
Good telling needs to be concrete and specific. It is quite easy to generalize or go
abstract in telling, especially for novice writers.
Tips
Showing. The American Heritage Dictionary defines "to show" as "to cause
or allow to be seen." In literature, showing is also referred to as dramatizing. If
something is shown, or dramatized, the reader is allowed to be an eyewitness (of
sorts) to the events of the story, novel or essay through the use of dialogue (what
characters say) and action (what characters do).
Telling. Also referred to as summary or narration, telling is used to directly
communicate or describe what is happening to the reader. That is, as a writer, you
can describe the setting (e.g., It was a dark and stormy night); you can describe
the characters (e.g., She had a face as broad and as innocent as a cabbage); and
you can even "tell the plot by summarizing what happens at a particular point.

• Concrete language (I

need to use concrete language when showing or telling our story. The key to create
a good character lies in those concrete words that can successfully demonstrate the
character's specific details, including his or her actions, behavior, attitudes, values
and feelings. Concreteness depends on the writer's ability to perceive, not merely to
see, and to translate those perceptions into concrete language. Concreteness can be
achieved by the use of adjectives, adverbs, nouns and especially verbs.
In the following two passages from "The Selfish Giant," we can notice that the
author uses concrete language (in bold) to create a live scene for readers such as the
sound that the Giant heard, the sight that the Giant saw and the feeling that the Giant
had about the sound and the sight. Without the use of concrete language, would the
two passages draw your attention or touch you?

One morning the Giant was lying awake in bed when he heard some lovely music. It
sounded so sweet to his ears that he thought it must be the King's musicians passing by.
It was really only a little linnet singing outside his window, but it was so long since he had
heard a bird sing in his garden that it seemed to him to be the most beautiful music in the
world. Then the Hail stopped dancing over his head, and the North Wind ceased roaring
and a delicious perfume came to him through the open casement.
He saw a most wonderful sight. Through a little hole in the wall the children had crept
in, and they were sitting in the branches of the trees. In every tree that he could see there
was a little child. And the trees were so glad to have the children back again that they
had covered themselves with blossoms, and were waving their arms gently above the
children's heads. The birds were flying about and twittering with delight, and the flowers
were looking up through the green grass and laughing.
A writer who doesn't use effective verbs can turn the most dramatic events into
a snooze. In the following passage from "The Selfish Giant," the author uses a series
of action verbs (in bold) to show what the Giant did after he became aware of his
selfishness. With these action verbs, we can picture the scene in our minds.
So he crept downstairs and opened the front door quite softly, and went out into the
garden. But when the children saw him they were so frightened that they all ran away, and
the garden became winter again. Only the little boy did not run, for his eyes were so full of
tears that he did not see the Giant coming. And the Giant stole up behind him and took
him gently in his hand, and put him up into the tree.
• Figurative language (I)
In addition to concrete language such as verbs, adjectives and nouns, effective
descriptions usually depend on a variety of figurative language (or figures of speech).
Let's examine the nature and functions of three figures of speech: simile, metaphor
and personification.
Simile makes a direct comparison frequently using such words as like or as. We
can find a good example in "The Selfish Giant": He was dressed in grey, and his breath
was like ice. This simile likens the Hail to ice.
Metaphor is an implied comparison. Instead of pointing to the likeness of two
otherwise unrelated concepts, metaphor states that one thing is another. Metaphor,
because it contains an implied rather than a stated comparison, is more complex.
Again we can find an example in "The Selfish Giant": "I have many beautiful flowers,'
he said, "but the children are the most beautiful flowers of all." The Giant considered
the children the most beautiful flowers of all, revealing his love toward them and his
Unit 2 Empathy and Justice
change from a selfish person to an unselfish person.
Personification gives a special kind of animation to objects, concepts, etc. Like
metaphors, personification makes an implicit comparison. In "The Selfish Giant," the
author uses a great deal of personification in describing the garden: The Snow covered
up the grass with her great white cloak, and the Frost painted all the trees silver. Then they
invited the North Wind to stay with them, and he came. He was wrapped in furs, and he
roared all day about the garden, and blew the chimney-pots down. In this example, the
author personifies snow, frost and the north wind, making them act like human beings.
Figurative language can add to the quality of your writing, making the words
more memorable. The writing is simply more fun. However, the use of clichés should
be limited. A cliché is an expression that has been used so much and is therefore
worn out. Examples includeỗDon't put off until tomorrow what you can get done
today!" and "It's raining cats and dogs!" Instead of using clichés, be original. Think of
new figures of speech to add interest to your narrative writing.

Part I: Learning the Skills
• What is setting?
The setting is the time and place in which a story occurs. The setting can be
imaginary, like the island Neverland in the story of Peter Pan, or can be real. The
setting can be determined by the story, or the story can be determined by the setting
Settings can set the parameters for a story. Even without knowing the plot of a story,
being given the location is helpful for readers to make assumptions about characters
and events. For example, in The Story of My Life (Chapter 4) (Text A of Unit 1), the
first sentence of the first paragraph (The most important day I remember in all my life
is the one on which my teacher, Anne Mansfield Sullivan, came to me.) and the first
sentence of the second paragraph (On the afternoon of that eventful day, I stood on
the porch, dumb, expectant.) arouse the reader' interest in knowing why that day was
important and what happened to Helen who stood on the porch. InạẠAfter Twenty
Years" (Text A of Unit 2), O. Henry starts the story with the sentence The policeman
on the beat moved up the avenue impressively. This sentence introduces the general
setting of the story-the avenue. Then the author describes the habitual action of a
policeman until he slowed his walk:
When about midway of a certain block the policeman suddenly slowed his walk. In the
doorway of a darkened hardware store a man leaned, with an unlighted cigar in his mouth.
As the policeman walked up to him the man spoke up quickly.
The policeman's stop brings out the specific setting and the protagonists of the
story. We really want to know what the man and the policeman are going to talk
about.

• What is the relationship between the setting and sensory details?
A key part of Sigmund Freud's theory of psychoanalysis has to do with the idea
of transference. The idea is that we commonly take emotions that we are feeling
and transfer them onto other people. This is exactly what we do in writing. We
take emotional meaning and transfer it onto people, places or things. Therefore,
with "Little Red Riding Hood," a walk in the woods becomes much more than just
that-it becomes filled with emotional as well as physical danger and the potential
loss of innocence. Therefore, in writing, we transfer complex emotions onto the
sensory objects and events we have chosen to render in the story. Hence, sensory
Unit 3 Growth and Maturity
details allow readers to put themselves in a particular setting mentally by forming
a picture in their mind. Without sensory details, readers would become bored and
cannot be emotionally connected to the story.
When we read the following paragraph, we can picture the scene in which a
blind young girl (Helen Keller) was acting and thinking with the aid of those sensory
details.

guessed vaguely from my mother's signs and from the hurrying to and fro in the house that

The afternoon sun penetrated the mass of honeysuckle that covered the porch, and fell
on my upturned face. My fingers lingered almost unconsciously on the familiar leaves and
blossoms which had just come forth to greet the sweet southern spring. I did not know
what the future held of-marvel or surprise for me. Anger and bitterness had preyed upon
me continually for weeks and a deep languor had succeeded this passionate struggle

• What is the relationship between the setting and characters?
The setting is an integral part of the whole story. Settings affect characters'
actions and feelings. It is often found that locations are used to provide clues to
a character's mood or as a means of externalizing his or her inner turmoil. If you
change the setting, you may have a fundamentally different story. For example, in "The
Necklace," five main settings are given, including Mathilde's apartment, Madame
Forestier's place, the palace of the ministry, a shop at the Palais-Royal and the
Champs-Elysees. Mathilde's fate altered with the changing of these settings.

Part II: Case Analysis
In some stories the setting is incidental, simply providing a backdrop for the action.
Stories that are primarily concerned with a character's thoughts and feelings-an inner
landscape-are not dependent on the setting. However, we often find that locations are
used to provide clues to a character's mood or as a means of externalizing inner turmoil.
In other stories the setting is integral. The change of the setting may result in another
story. A carefully realized setting can develop a reader's belief in the story through the
inclusion of details that provide clues to a place or period. Read the following texts and
consider the questions: Is the setting integral to the story or merely a backdrop? How does
the setting influence the mood of the characters or highlight the conflict? What is the
significance of the setting? How do shifts in the setting impact on the story?

Part III: Language Study
• Sensory details
In Units 1 and 2, we have learned that the characters express their feelings through
what they say and what they do. In this unit, we have learned that settings can also
Unit 3 Growth and Maturity
be greatly helpful in terms of portraying characters and delivering a story's theme.
When you write a setting, it is better to call upon more, if not all the senses. The first
impression the author gives the reader is often what a place looks like-what the
narrator sees. For example, in The Story of My Life (Chapter 4) (Text A of Unit 1), the
author presents us the growth or change in herself mainly through physical interactions
between herself and her surroundings. Likewise, in "The Selfish Giant" (Text B of Unit 2),
sentences such as "It [music] sounded so sweet to his ears that he thought it must be the
King's musicians passing by" vividly demonstrate how much the Giant wanted to keep
the garden as his own. Here are some words that can help to show the five senses:
1) SMELL: rotten, spicy, balmy, musty, putrid, savory, acidic, pungent...
2) TASTE: salty, peppery, repulsive, tart, tangy, delicious, luscious...
3) TOUCH: gentle, aching, tingling, mangy, velvety, rubbery, itchy...
4) SOUND: thundering, murmur, crackle, soothing, hissing, shrill, yelp...
5) SIGHT: angular, blurry, transparent, dim, foggy, fluorescent, glowing...

• Concrete language (II)
In Unit 2, we discussed the importance of concrete language in writing. Concrete
words improve the quality of writing. Using concrete words is a good way to make
your description (or telling) believable, visualized and readable. For example, in "Too
Soon a Woman," the author uses simple but concrete words to show us the difficult
situation (here the setting) that the boy's family and Mary experienced:
We left the home place behind, mile by slow mile, heading for the mountains, across
the prairie where the wind blew forever.
At first there were four of us with the one-horse wagon and its skimpy load. Pa and I
walked, because I was a big boy of eleven. My two little sisters romped and trotted until
they got tired and had to be boosted up into the wagon bed
Concrete words can be adjectives, adverbs, nouns and especially verbs. Whenever
you try to create a believable scene, you are doing some description. A good description
can give readers a clear and vivid picture of the things or events recorded.

Part I: Learning the Skills
Example 1
• What is point of view?
In narrative writing, the author decides what the reader will see and know from
the story through choices of point of view. Point of view can generally be defined as
who tells the story, how the story is told or the way in which it is narrated. The view can
be limited to characters' actions or extended to their inner thoughts and feelings. The
point of view can offer insight into a single character or expand to everyone involved
in the story. When you read a story, you may ask: What is the point of view? Does the
point of view provide me with adequate information or would the story be better with
an alternative? How does the point of view work to reveal the characters?
• What are the types of point of view?
Different people come up with different classifications about the types of point of
view in writing. First person (I) and third person (he/she/they) are more frequently used
in narrative writing. Second person is possible and is more commonly seen in business
writing and technical writing, and sometimes appears in letters and speeches.
1. First person point of view
In the first person point of view (or personal narration), the narrator, "I, can be
the author or one of the characters. This kind of narration offers the reader a chance
to get an insight into the character's feelings or thoughts. Read the following examples
and find out what the "I" refers to in each excerpt.
Early on the morning of August 19, 1946, I was born under a clear sky after a violent
summer storm to a widowed mother in the Julia Chester Hospital in Hope, a town of about
six thousand in southwest Arkansas, thirty-three miles east of the Texas border at Texarkana.
My mother named me William Jefferson Blythe Ill after my father, William Jefferson Blythe
Jr., one of nine children of a poor farmer in Sherman, Texas, who died when my father was
seventeen. According to his sisters, my father always tried to take care of them, and he
grew up to be a handsome, hardworking, fun-loving man. He met my mother at Tri-State
Hospital in Shreveport, Louisiana, in 1943, when she was training to be a nurse. Many times
when I was growing up, I asked Mother to tell me the story of their meeting, courting and
marriage.

when mine opened on it. There is something strange to me, even now, in the reflection

She was broken-hearted, and so was I, and we cried; but she comforted me as well as she

The first excerpt is from former U.S. President Bill Clinton's autobiography My
Life. His father died before he was born. Therefore, he said that "I was born under

The third excerpt is from the American writer Mark Twain's short story "A Dog's

2. Second person point of view
With the second person point of view, the narrator tells the story to another
character using "you," and the story is being told through the addressee's point
of view. In narrative writing, the second person point of view is used much less
compared with the first person or third person point of view. Sometimes, it might
be "an inverted first person, that is, a first person narrator refers himself or herself
as "you." Or this "you" appears as part of the monologue or letters. Occasionally, this

The choice of second person point of view usually shows that the author has a

3. Third person point of view
In narrative writing, third person point of view is frequently used. It can be
further divided into three subcategories: objective point of view, omniscient point of
view and limited omniscient point of view.
1) Objective point of view
With the objective point of view, the author simply describes what happens
without stating more than can be inferred from the story's actions and dialogue. The
author never discloses anything about what the characters think or feel, remaining a
detached observer. Simply speaking, the action speaks for itself. Read the following
excerpt and think about how the story is presented.
"Where's Papa going with the ax?" said Fern to her mother as they were setting the
table for breakfast.
"Out to the hog house," replied Mrs. Arable. "Some pigs were born last night"

"Well," said her mother, "one of the pigs is a runt. It's very small and weak, and it will
never amount to anything. So your father has decided to do away with it."
"Do away with it?" shrieked Fern. "You mean kill it? Just because it's smaller than the

Fern pushed a chair out of the way and ran outdoors. The grass was wet and the earth
smelled of springtime. Fern's sneakers were sopping by the time she caught up with her
father.
"Please don't kill it!" she sobbed. "It's unfair."
Mr. Arable stopped walking.
"Fern," he said gently, "you will have to learn to control yourself."

In this excerpt, a little pig was born on Fern's farm. Her father wanted to kill
it because it was so weak. Fern, a little girl, was sympathetic toward the little pig.
But the author does not tell us what the little girl was thinking. Instead, the author
presents Fern's and her parents' actions and words. The reader will get the message
just from the author's description of the scene.
2) Omniscient point of view
Similar to the objective point of view, the author does not participate in the
action of the story in omniscient point of view narrative writing. However, the author
appears to know everything. Using this kind of viewpoint, the author can enter the
mind of any of the characters and reveal their feelings and thoughts. This method was
once quite popular because it gives the writer more freedom with all the characters in
the narrative and, therefore, gives the reader more information about the characters.
Read the following excerpt and see how the narrator reveals the feelings and thoughts
of the characters.
Tom begged her to pluck up hope again, and she said she could not. He fell to blaming
and abusing himself for getting her into this miserable situation; this had a better effect.
She said she would try to hope again, she would get up and follow wherever he might lead
if only he would not talk like that any more. For he was no more to blame than she, she
said. So they moved on again-aimlessly-simply at random-all they could do was to
move, keep moving.
By-and-by, Tom took Becky's candle and blew it out. This economy meant so much!
Words were not needed. Becky understood, and her hope died again. She knew that Tom
had a whole candle and three or four pieces in his pockets-yet he must economize.
By-and-by, fatigue began to assert its claims; the children tried to pay attention, for it
was dreadful to think of sitting down when time was grown to be so precious, moving, in
some direction, in any direction, was at least progress and might bear fruit; but to sit down
was to invite death and shorten its pursuit.
At last Becky's frail limbs refused to carry her farther. She sat down. Tom rested with
her, and they talked of home, and the friends there, and the comfortable beds and, above
all, the light! Becky cried, and Tom tried to think of some way of comforting her, but all his
encouragements were grown threadbare with use, and sounded like sarcasms. Fatigue
bore so heavily upon Becky that she drowsed off to sleep. Tom was grateful. He sat looking

into her drawn face and saw it grow smooth and natural under the influence of pleasant
dreams; and by-and-by a smile dawned and rested there. The peaceful face reflected
somewhat of peace and healing into his own spirit, and his thoughts wandered away to
bygone times and dreamy memories.
—The Adventure of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain
In this excerpt, two characters are mentioned: Tom and Becky. The reader can
know not only the two characters' actions and words, but also what they were thinking,
for instance, "She [Becky] knew that Tom had a whole candle... yet he must economize"
and "Tom tried to think of some way of comforting her... Tom was grateful." All this is
made known to the reader directly through the narrator's observation as if he were on
the scene and knew everything. This is very typical omniscient point of view.
Let's look at another example:
Mary had liked to look at her mother from a distance and she had thought her very
pretty, but as she knew very little of her she could scarcely have been expected to love her
or to miss her very much when she was gone. She did not miss her at all, in fact, and as she
was a self-absorbed child she gave her entire thought to herself, as she had always done. If
she had been older she would no doubt have been very anxious at being left alone in the
world, but she was very young, and as she had always been taken care of, she supposed
she always would be. What she thought was that she would like to know if she was going
to nice people, who would be polite to her and give her her own way as her Ayah and the
other native servants had done.
-The Secret Garden by Frances Hodgson Burnett
Mary spent the first few years of her life in India with her parents, who died of
an epidemic and she had to be taken care of by others. From this excerpt, we could
understand Mary's thoughts and feelings. This is made possible through the use of
omniscient point of view.
3) Limited omniscient point of view
In most cases, it is impossible for one to know all the mental activities of all
others. Therefore, one disadvantage of the omniscient point of view is its credibility.
To avoid this problem, some authors choose the limited omniscient point of view.
That is, the third person reveals the point of view of one or two characters but not
that of all the characters. Therefore, the narrator's knowledge is limited to the specific
character(s). Read the following excerpt and see how much the narrator knows about
the character.

Jonas was careful about language. Not like his friend, Asher, who talked too fast and mixed
things up, scrambling words and phrases until they were barely recognizable and often very funny.
Jonas grinned, remembering the morning that Asher had dashed into the classroom,
late as usual, arriving breathlessly in the middle of the chanting of the morning anthem.
When the class took their seats at the conclusion of the patriotic hymn, Asher remained
standing to make his public apology as was required
"I apologize for inconveniencing my learning community." Asher ran through the
standard apology phrase rapidly, still catching his breath. The Instructor and class waited
patiently for his explanation. The students had all been grinning, because they had listened
to Asher's explanations so many times before.
-The Giver by Lois Lowry
In this excerpt, the author describes what happened from the memory of one
character: Jonas. The reader can enter Jonas' mind when they read about his memory
of Asher's apology. Meanwhile, the author restricts herself from seeing things from
other characters' eyes. For instance, here the reader does not really know what Asher
was thinking or what the instructor was thinking. Therefore, we can say that the
author is using a limited omniscient point of view.

Part III: Language Study
• Precise word choice
In writing, precise words can work effectively in describing what the author
intends to convey to the reader. At the same time, you should be clear that good word
choices do not mean that you always have to use those big or elaborate words. A
frequent use of unusual words would greatly increase the reader's load and might
kill their interest in your writing. Another problem is the overuse of certain
words or phrases. Too much repetition (unless for specific rhetorical purposes)
would weaken your writing. Good use of words means using the right words
to say the right thing in the right way. In this section, we are going to see some
examples and see how the authors strengthen their writing by effectively using
the specific words or phrases.
It was a bright, cold day, the ground covered with a sleet that had frozen so that it
seemed as if all the bare trees, the bushes, the cut brush and all the grass and the bare
ground had been varnished with ice. I took the young Irish setter for a walk up the road and
along a frozen creek, but it was difficult to stand or walk on the glassy surface and the red
dog slipped and slithered and I fell twice, hard, once dropping my gun and having it slide
away over the ice.
-"A Day's Wait" by Ernest Hemingway
In this paragraph, the author uses a variety of specific words and phrases such as
sleet, frozen, bare, varnished with ice and glassy to create a vivid cold winter day.
Sleet refers to frozen raindrops. If there is a sleet, the ground will be all covered with
frozen raindrops. Then the author mentions the "bare" trees to help enhance a winter
image-bare trees means trees without leaves, with only the branches and tree trunk
standing there, showing the solemn winter. Next, the author uses a metaphor to say that it
seemed as if everything had been "varnished with ice. The word varnish means to apply
a hard transparent cover on something. Here it means everything is covered with glossy,
hard and transparent ice. Just imagine what it is like in your mind! As it continued, the
narrator walked along "a frozen creek" which tells the reader more about how cold it
was. The author also uses other ways to describe the icy and cold world, such as"... it was
difficult to stand or walk on the glassy surface..." The word glassy vividly tells how slippery
100 Writing Critically 1
it might be to walk on such an icy road. The author then uses another three specific words
to further strengthen the reader's impression of the cold icy world: slip, slither and slide. To
be specific, slide means to move smoothly along a surface; slip has the meaning of moving
involuntarily usually because of wet or icy road conditions; slither means to slip or slide
unsteadily. These words also share similar sounds, creating the image of the slippery road
conditions. The slippery road condition is also reflected when the author uses expressions
such as fell twice, hard. Combining all of these, the author presents a vivid image of a
cold and icy winter day.

• Narrative tense
When we narrate, we use a combination of tenses to show the order events
occurred in. If we keep writing about events as they happened, that is, one event
followed by the next, the writing may sound abstract and boring. For example,
ạI went cycling; I was with my family; we saw a car; the car drove fast; the car
overtook us; it hit the tractor." The sentence could be rewritten as: "While I was
cycling with my family, we saw a car which drove so fast that it hit the tractor soon
after it overtook usẠỊiBy changing tenses and rearranging the events, we are able to
describe events more effectively. Read the following passage and consider the use of
tenses.

holes, and think that if things had been different they might have made a much better
showing, the greater part accept their lot, if not with serenity, at all events with resignation.
They are like train-cars travelling forever on the selfsame rails. They go backwards and
forwards, backwards and forwards, inevitably, till they can go no longer and then are sold
as scrap-iron. It is not often that you find a man who has boldly taken the course of his life

That was why I was curious to meet Thomas Wilson. It was an interesting and a bold thing
he had done. Of course the end was not yet and until the experiment was concluded it was
impossible to call it successful. But from what I had heard it seemed he must be an odd sort
of fellow and I thought I should like to know him. I had been told he was reserved, but I had a

In the above passage, the author uses a variety of tenses. The first paragraph
mainly uses the present tense and the second mainly the past tense. There is a
contrast between these two paragraphs in terms of tense. Why is this so?
The first paragraph is about the narrator's general comment about life, something
that the narrator considered as truth. It applies to all: "Most people... lead the lives...
and think..." Here the author uses the present perfect tense in the first sentence: "
… that
circumstances have thrust upon them?' Here we see the order of events. Because of the
existing circumstances, people will live a certain kind of life. Besides tenses, subjective
mood is also used in this paragraph. All these together help enhance the narrator's point
of view: Generally speaking, most people cannot live the life the way they want.
In the second paragraph, the author switches to the past tense. Here the narrator
was talking about a particular person and a particular case. He started to talk about
something that happened in the past, telling the reader about a person he had known
and how this person led his life differently from others as an example of the point he
put forward at the end of the first paragraph.
On top of other things, the different choices of tense in these two paragraphs
help the author compare the general situation and the specific case he is going to
elaborate in more detail in the following part of the work.

Part I: Learning the Skills
• What is theme?
Theme is the central meaning of a narrative. It has been called the worldview,
philosophy, message or moral lesson within a story. The theme of a story is the most
important thing the author wants the reader to get from the story.
Themes can be explicit or implicit. Read the following examples and find out the
theme of each example.
Example 1
Michael Jordan
In his sophomore year of high school, Michael Jordan tried out for the varsity basketball
team at Laney High School in Wilmington, North Carolina. But at five feet and eleven inches
tall, Jordan was believed by the coach to be too short to play at that level, so Jordan was
cut from the team. Jordan didn't let this obstacle defeat him. In fact, it pushed him to work
even harder. He trained vigorously and grew another four inches the following summer.
110 Writing Critically 1
When he finally made the varsity squad, Jordan averaged 25 points a game and went on to
become one of the greatest basketball players in history.
Example 2
The Wild Boar and the Fox
A Wild Boar stood under a tree and rubbed his tusks against the trunk. A Fox passing by
asked him why he sharpened his teeth when there was no danger threatening from either
huntsman or hound. He repliedạI do it advisedly, for it would never do to have to sharpen
my weapons just at the time I ought to be using themịỊại
Example 3
The Thieves and the Cock
Some thieves broke into a house and found nothing but a Cock, whom they stole, and
got off as fast as they could. Upon arriving at home they prepared to kill the Cock, who thus
pleaded for his life: "Pray spare me; I am very serviceable to men. I wake them up in the very
early morning to their work.""That is the very reason why we must the more kill you, they
replied, "for when you wake your neighbors, you entirely put an end to our business.
The safeguards of virtue are hateful to those with evil intentions.
Example 1 is a piece of non-fiction narrative writing. Examples 2 and 3 are from
Aesop's Fables. Examples 1 and 2 do not explicitly offer the theme. Yet the moral of
each is very clear: The message in Example 1 is "to be persistent and never give up"
while Example 2 tells that one should always be prepared. In Example 3, there is an
explicit moral message at the end.
As can be seen, themes are not unique to fictional literature. Any form of
storytelling, including movies, television series, songs and poetry, can (and should)
contain thematic elements.
All the elements, such as characterization, plot and setting, work together to
construct the theme. The theme is expressed through what the characters say, do
and think, and through everything that takes place within the story. The theme
is also revealed in how the plot and setting of the narrative are constructed and
presented.

• What are common themes in narrative writing?
The theme of a story is the most important thing the author wants readers to
understand. It is the author's thoughts about a general belief of how things are or how
they should be. Examples of themes include coming of age, nostalgia or loneliness,
redemption, sacrifice, betrayal, loyalty, greed, justice, oppression, revenge and love.
Themes might also involve types of conflict: between the individual and society, the
individual and nature, the individual and oneself, and the individual and technology.
By telling the reader what the story is about, the theme expresses the ideas or
issues raised within the story. Keep in mind that most stories have multiple themes.
For example, in Harry Potter, the most significant themes are love and good vs. evil.
However, there are also themes of friendship, sacrifice and redemption. One theme
might stretch across an entire series, while other themes appear in one book or one
chapter of the series. The following are some examples showing different themes. All
these excerpts are from Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets by J. K. Rowling.

• How is theme revealed through narration?
Themes are one of the most fundamental aspects in narrative writing. These
themes often have their roots in human motivations, feelings and relationships.
Themes themselves could be rather dull, preachy or abstract, such as good vs. evil,
betrayal and loss, altruism, self-sacrifice and the corrupting nature of power. But
themes provide the foundation on which a story rests and themes are the soil from
which all stories grow.
The theme of a narrative is revealed to the reader through different techniques.
In general, it could be implicit or explicit. By "implicit," it means that the author is not
directly telling the reader what the themes would be. Instead, they are woven into the
plot development and characterization. For instance, after we read the above three
excerpts, we know that there are several themes revealed to us. In the first excerpt,
we can see the theme of friendship. It is demonstrated to us through the use of plot
design. That is, when Harry was locked up by his uncle, Ron came to rescue him. It is
also revealed through the use of dialogue between Harry and Ron. In the second and
third excerpts, themes such as love, greed and courage are also revealed through the
development of the plot, particularly the dialogue between the protagonist and the
antagonist. Besides this implicit way of delivering themes, it might also be possible to
be more explicit about the theme or the point that the author wants to share with his
or her readers. For example, in Excerpt 3 on Pages 102 and 103, the author indicates
the theme in the first paragraph. The author shows us a very ordinary interaction a
father had with his daughter, who instructed her father about how to properly meet a
kid in "the twenty-first century." The theme is mentioned at the very beginning: The
choices of the children not only depend on their own efforts and attitudes but also
depend on men-and American society-respecting and accommodating the choices
they make. The father respected his daughter's idea about meeting a kid according to
his or her ideas.
Other writing techniques might also affect how themes are presented. For
instance, if a story is presented through only one point of view, the reader can
conclude that this character's interpretation of events represents the only important
interpretation of the narrative. On the other hand, if a story is presented from
multiple points of view, the reader might have to interpret it on multiple levels and
from multiple perspectives. The theme may also be revealed by the narrator. A third-
person omniscient narrator who presents various characters' thoughts and feelings
may reveal a more abstract and broader theme than a third-person limited narrator
who presents only one character's thoughts and feelings.
116 Writing Critically 1
• How to develop and interpret themes in narrative writing?
There is a good chance that themes will manifest themselves even if you put
no special effort into their development. In fact, themes are always so closely tied
to human nature that it is almost impossible to tell a story without a theme of some
kind. But if you approach a theme with intent (even vague intent), your work will
have greater depth and meaning.
In most narrative writing, themes shouldn't be overly obvious. If you're working
on a theme involving sacrifice, you don't want to have your characters making
sacrifices all the time. Themes work best when they are subtle in most cases.
Since themes can contain messages and morals, you should make a conscious effort
not to force your personal beliefs and values onto your readers. There is a difference
between making a statement and being preachy. Most readers don't like novels that
preach at them. In fact, some themes work best when they are presented as questions
and the reader gets to experience contrary viewpoints. For example, we all accept that
stealing is wrong, but we feel differently about it when a small starving child is stealing a
piece of bread. After identifying a story's theme, the reader can make conclusions about
the story. These conclusions are the reader's interpretation of the text.

Part III: Language Study
• Figurative language (Il)
Figurative language refers to words or expressions with a meaning that is
different from their daily or literal interpretation. Writers ornament their writing
with figurative language to make it more entertaining or to clarify the meaning they
intend to convey. Figurative language is very common in poetry, but is also used
in prose and non-fiction writing. In Unit 2, we briefly learned about three types of
figurative language, and in this unit, we are going to learn more.
1. Alliteration
Alliteration refers to the repetition of the same sounds or the same kinds of
sounds at the beginning of the words. For example, in Story 2 on Page 135, there
are several examples of alliteration such as "wide whispering woods" and "fearful
frenziedẠỊiAlliteration creates an atmosphere in rhythm, thus making the narrative or
Unit 5 Dream and Faith 131
description more vivid.
2. Hyperbole
Exaggerating, often in a humorous way, is known as hyperbole. For example:
• On the sidewalk Soapy began to yell drunken gibberish at the top of his harsh voice. He
danced, howled, raved, and otherwise disturbed the welkin.
In this example, Soapy thought of the idea of making noises so that he might
be arrested because of "disorderly conduct." Therefore, he was making such a fuss of
himself that he disturbed the sky or universe. "Welkin" is a word often used in poetry
with the meaning of "the sky, the vault of heaven?' Of course, it is impossible for him
to make that kind of noise. It is just exaggeration. He wanted to draw the attention of
a cop who was nearby but failed. Here are more examples:
• Then she reached down, picked the boy up by his shirt front, and shook him until his
teeth rattled
• My eyes widened at the sight of the mile-high ice cream cones we were having for dessert.
3. Onomatopoeia
Onomatopoeia names an action or a thing according to what it sounds like. For
example, "The bees buzz angrily when their hive is disturbed." The sounds made by
the bees could almost be heard when the word "buzz' is pronounced. The following
are more examples.
• The cow mooed when it saw a passing train.
• Birds twittered and tweeted...
• The horse's hooves clip-clopped on the cobblestones.
4. Understatement
In contrast with hyperbole, which greatly exaggerates the truth, understatement
deliberately makes a situation less important or serious than it is. For example:
• I have to have this operation. It isn't very serious. I have this tiny little tumor on the brain.
In this example, this "I" first mentioned an operation that was necessary for
him or her because he or she had to have that. But then he or she described it as not
serious. The last sentence reveals the seriousness of the problem: This "I" actually got
a tumor on the brain. Yet, he or she tried to downplay the possible consequences. This
is further strengthened by two adjectives: "tiny" and "little." This description would
be a sharp contrast with what we usually describe a tumor on the brain, thus greatly
enhances the characterization of the speaker.

5. Simile
• "No cop for youse," said the waiter, with a voice like butter cakes and an eye like the
cherry in a Manhattan cocktail.
By comparing two elements, the descriptive effect is enhanced, thus making it
more impressive. For instance, by describing the waiter as having a voice like "butter
cakes" and an eye like "the cherry in a Manhattan cocktail," the author tells us what
the waiter is like-very unpleasant and unfriendly. Comparing the voice with butter
cakes and his eyes with a cherry in a cocktail is fresh and creative. The following are
more examples of simile:
• He arose, joint by joint, as a carpenter's rule opens, and beat the dust from his
clothes.
• My love is like a red, red rose.
• He wasn't frightened exactly, but he was as anxious as a fish out of water to find his
family before evening.
6. Metaphor
• With the young woman playing the clinging ivy to his oak Soapy walked past the
policeman, overcome with gloom.
In this sentence, the "ivy" refers to the woman and the "oak" refers to Soapy. The
woman clung to Soapy so tightly that she looked like ivy clinging to an oak. The use
of metaphor makes the image very clear. Here are more examples:
• Alice was thrilled when her idea began to bear fruit.
• The boss thundered into the room.
7. Personification
• For years the hospitable Blackwell's had been his winter quarters.
The word "hospitable" is usually used to describe a person who treats his or her
guest with warmth. But here it refers to a prison, which is usually not modified by
such a word. Thus, a combination of personification and irony creates a strong impact
on the reader. Here are more examples:

Part I: Learning the Skills
• What is plot?
Plot is a series of events and thoughts arranged to reveal their dramatic and
emotional significance. Plot is not just a sequence of chronological events. Rather,
plot implies that there is a meaningful relationship among the events. Plot is often
characterized by a conflict, a struggle between two or more opposing forces. The
conflict may be internal (person vs. self) or external (person vs. person; person vs.
nature; person vs. society; person vs. fate). A story may have more than one conflict.
The simplest view of plot is that stories have a beginning, a middle and an
ending. For example, at the beginning of Perrault's Cinderella, a young girl was faced
with a lifetime of drudgery and decision. Her fairy godmother arrived in the middle
of the tale to offer her some sparkling alternatives. Cinderella ultimately discovered
the old adage "If the shoe fits, wear it" and lived happily ever after with her prince.
More sophisticated views of plot show the sequence of time in related episodes.
For example, in the story of Mufaro's Beautiful Daughters: An African Tale by John
Steptoe, the polarity of the actions and reactions of two sisters leads them into
very different futures. The gentle and generous Nyasha met and married her king,
while the bad-tempered Manyara was left to be a servant in her sister's household.
Steptoe foreshadows the ultimate events through Manyara's dire, though misguided,
predictions and the early appearance of the young king in a variety of symbolic
guises. Because they are fairy tales, both stories are marked by the "rule of three."
Cinderella attended the ball three nights before her prince discovered her identity,
while Nyasha must face three trials before she and her king were married.
• What are the five elements of plot?
Gustav Freytag, a German dramatist and novelist, divides the plot into five elements:
exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution/denouement.
Exposition refers to the introduction of a story, the background information
140 Writing Critically 1
needed to properly understand the story. This part can include the main characters),
the setting and so forth. The initial event triggering the rest of the story also occurs in
this part. For instance, in the Father and Son pictures, the son broke the windows and
then ran away from his home because his father was mad at him. That would be the
exposition element of the plot.
Rising action refers to the events leading up to the climax. For example, in the
above story, the father's initial anger with his son turned into worries when the son
ran away and did not come back when it was getting late. He even went out to look
for his son. These events are the "rising action."
The climax is the most exciting part of the story. This is where all the rising action
finally reaches its peak. For example, in the Father and Son pictures, the climax occurs
when the second window was broken. According to the previous information in the
exposition, the reader might assume that the son was going to be punished more
seriously, thus making the story more intriguing.
The falling action deals with events occurring right after the climax. These
events are usually the after-effects of the climax.
Resolution, which is sometimes called denouement, is the end of the falling
action and the conclusion to the story. There is usually a release of dramatic tension
and anxiety. It can also be the part that reveals the final outcome of its conflicts or
the solution of its mysteries. At the same time, stories sometimes have endings with
questions left unanswered. In the above story, the father was so happy to find his son
again that he held him tight instead of punishing him.
These five elements of plot structure can vary slightly, but for the most part it
is the gradual build-up of events, the climax, followed by a resolution. It is often

• What is the role of conflict in narrative writing?
Conflict is the key to plotting a great script. It defines the parameters of the story,
Unit 6 Conflict and Harmony 145
helps to generate tension and suspense and shapes the audience's experience of the
characters. When conflict is properly developed, the story has the best chance of
fulfilling the audience's expectations.
1. The main conflict
Every plot needs a main conflict for the protagonist to face. This conflict defines
the basic parameters of the plot and raises the dramatic question of the story (i.e.,
whether the protagonist will prevail or not) that is answered at the climax. It contains
the protagonist's main objective and the main obstacle.
2. Characters in conflict
In most cases, the characters (especially in the protagonist/antagonist axis,
but in other character relationships, too) involved in a conflict are rival characters
who usually contrast with each other. However, opposing characters aren't always
antagonists; sometimes, they just represent opposing ideas. These opposing
characters make the meaning of the story clearer because they reveal contradictory
traits and values.
When creating characters, writers need to clearly define their opposing
characteristics and values, especially for the protagonist and the antagonist. Contrast
them not only in what they do and what they want to achieve, but also in what they
think.
3. Suspense in conflict
The sort of suspense created by conflict is what Jessamyn West is supposed to
have called "willy wonty' the reader's uncertainty as to whether a character "will" or
"won't" commit an act, decide a matter, do a deed, choose one instead of another, give
up or go on, marry the girl or let her go. "Willy wonty" can be a wonderfully effective
way of getting the reader to read on: It is the suspenseful reaction at its simplest.
But to be effective, the situation of the conflict must be developed so that the forces,
weights or values on each side are more or less balanced. If we are to have any interest
in whether a character will or won't, then the reasons for him to do it or not to do it,
the pressures and pulls on him in both directions, must be fairly equally presented.
All that is well enough, but the difficulty is that the more successfully the conflict is
developed, the harder it is to resolve. The more uncertain a reader is made to become
as to what the outcome of a story is going to be, the less likely it is that he's going to
be convinced by the ending when it finally arrives. In both cases the writer and the
reader are working against each other, and also trying to outguess each other.

Part III: Language Study
• Cohesion
In writing, every writer wishes to make their points clear, with logical links between
the various points, thus making their writing easy to read. It can be said that cohesion is
the "glue" that joins one's ideas together to form a cohesive whole. According to Halliday
and Hasan, there are six main ways that cohesion is created in a text. These are reference,
substitution, lexis, ellipsis, cohesive nouns and conjunction.
Reference is a way of creating cohesion using determiners (e.g., this, that, these,
those) or pronouns (e.g., him, them, me, your, their, hers, which, who, whose). This
type of cohesion can also be achieved comparatively with words or phrases like
similarly, likewise and less. Here are some examples:
• Tom went to the fancy dress party, and he made his costume himself
• The disabled climber knew how difficult the climb would be at 2,880 meters. This
ascent, at such an altitude, had defeated many others.
• My room is small while hers is quite spacious.
• When the big white horse first came to the Provincale Milk Company he didn't have a
name. (lext B)
• Pierre used to boast that he didn't need reins-he never touched them. (Text B)
Substitution uses a word or a phrase to replace a word or a phrase used earlier. For
instance, the one(s) and the same/a same can be used to replace nouns (e.g., I like your new
cup. I'm going to buy a same one). Verbs can be replaced by do/does/did/done (e.g., The
authorities said they had acted, but nobody believed they had done). In oral English, whole
clauses can be replaced by so or not (e.g., I hope so/not). Here are more examples:
160 Writing Critically 1
• I need to buy some new shoes and those blue ones look lovely!
• The customer demonstrated outside the store, but he did not want to do so
• The winters can be wet and cold in London. The same is unhappily also true for the summers.
• He had been far from the scene of accident, and did not even know there had been
one. (Text A)
• No one knew Prince Edward Street as well as did Pierre Dupin, for Pierre had delivered
milk to the families on the street for thirty years now. (Text B)
Lexis is a way of creating cohesion by using synonyms (e.g., beautiful for lovely)
and hyponyms and superordinates (e.g., daffodil, rose and daisy are all hyponyms of the
superordinate flower). Lexical chains are created in a text by using words in the same lexical
set (e.g., army, soldiers, barracks, weapons). These techniques allow for the central themes to
be reiterated in a way that avoids monotony for the reader. Here are more examples:
• The art gallery was exhibiting all his paintings, but not the sculpture or his early
etchings.
• The players gathered on the pitch and kicked the ball around, before playing in earnest
• The students attending the lecture all took notes and asked a lot of questions.
• Pierre had a remarkable memory. When he arrived at the stable he'd always remember
to tell Jacques. (Text B)
Ellipsis is the act of leaving out one or more words that are not necessary for
understanding a phrase or a sentence (e.g.» John can type and I can ‹type>, too!; I don't want
to go out, do you ‹want to go out>?). Look at the following sentences and see whether you can
understand them while some words and expressions are omitted. Here are more examples:
• Ann was quite happy to handle the snake, although the others did not want to
• Here is the deck of cards, now take any four.
• I wanted to take another chocolate, but I knew I must not
• And yet she had loved him-sometimes. Often she had not. (Text A)
• Pierre's huge walrus mustache was pure white now and Joseph didn't lift his knees so
high or raise his head quite as much. (Text B)
Cohesive nouns are a kind of lexical reference. They can summarize many words
in one (e.g., attitude, solution, difficulty), therefore, they have been called "umbrella
nouns." They are used to signal what is to come (e.g., the problem to be discussed), or
what can refer back (e.g., the issue mentioned above). Here are more examples:
• Over a million dollars was spent last year. This investment was needed and was wisely spent.
• The two cars collided on the flyover. However, nobody was hurt in the accident.
• The children were always fighting, but no one seemed concerned about the problem.
