Unity reters to the oneness of your writing. The writing should have one focus
of a central idea or theme. Read the following short paragraph, and figure out which
sentence does not belong to this paragraph.
The most embarrassing moment of my sophomore year was how I earned my
nickname, Crash. It all started right after school when I turned onto the busiest street by
the school. First I pulled up right behind a truck at a stop sign. It was such a fine day. After
a second, I heard my friend Tom shout at me and tell me that I was so close that I was
going to hit the truck in front of me. I retorted that he should be careful himself because
he was hanging out of the window. Distracted, I thought the long line of traffic had started
to move, but it hadn't. In the blink of an eye I hit the back of the truck in front of me.

I never did hear the end of what had happened that day.
In this narrative paragraph, the narrator was talking about his most embarrassing
moment: how he had a traffic accident. Almost all of the sentences center around
the traffic accident: the traffic at that time, how his friend's shout distracted him,
the accidental collision with the truck and even the fact that his friend made fun of
him because of the accident. This indicates the unity of this paragraph. However, the
sentence "It was such a fine day" has nothing to do with the embarrassing moment
and should be deleted.

Part I: Learning the Skills
• What is style?
Every author has his or her own style, using literary devices in a particular way
that makes his or her writing recognizable. Style is usually confined to the elements
of language: words, syntax, punctuation and so on-everything from the simple
mechanics to the rhetoric that may reflect a given author's originality. Authors make
stylistic choices to set the mood of their stories, reveal characters and give voice to
their individual personalities.
Style is only one aspect of narration; it contributes only as it works with the
other aspects of narration. The interconnections are throughout, as always. The point
of view will have a determining effect on style, and be determined by it: Whoever
is seeing or telling the story must see and talk in a way that works with all the rest.
This, of course, brings us to the aspect of characterization: The sorts of characters
the author creates will speak the language of his or her world. What "happens" to
the author, the plots of his or her stories, will be the sorts of things that happen to
those sorts of characters in those sorts of places-wherever it is or whatever it is like
there-for the setting, too, will be determined by its relation to all the other aspects
of the author's world.
With regard to style, you could ask:
• What are some of the stylistic choices made by the author? Does the author make
use of a wide variety of stylistic devices or limit the selection to only a few?
• Why is the author's style so recognizable?
• How do specific choices expand or diminish the story?
• How do the stylistic choices in one story compare or contrast with those in other
stories?
Now consider this story opening:

Why does the author write it in this way? She uses "The hour was late" rather
than "It was late," and instead of "all the bears were tired," she repeats "was tired"

• What is tone?
Tone indicates the author's attitude toward his or her subject. Integrally linked to
style, tone not only reveals character(s), setting, plot and theme, but also highlights
the author's feelings about how these literary elements should play out. Tone can be
humorous, serious, affectionate, warm, cool, condescending or even sarcastic. When
you discuss tone you might ask:
• What is the tone used in this particular passage or about this particular character?
• What does the tone reveal about the author?
• Is the tone maintained throughout the story or does it shift depending on the
scene or the character?
• How is the tone reflected in stylistic choices?
In old-fashioned fiction, it is relatively easy to detect the author's tone. In the
omniscient point-of-view method, especially, the author would obtrude his or her
presence and make his or her comments on the action directly. The commentary
might be ironic in tone, but is more likely to be sentimental or didactic. In
contemporary fiction, the author is often conspicuously absent-especially in the
Unit 7 Ethnicity and Identity 169
first-person and third-person point-of-view methods. It is often far more difficult to
decide just what an author feels about the characters and their behavior.
Thus the more old-fashioned methods tend toward clarity and sympathy-a
kind of subjectivity on the author's part that creates a feeling of involvement. Newer
methods tend toward ambiguity and irony-a kind of objectivity on the author's part
that creates a feeling of detachment.
In short, to write a successful short story, the author needs to create a
recognizable individual "world" with the help of style and tone. In the previous
units, you may have noticed the distinct styles of O. Henry, Ernest Hemingway, Jack
London, Guy de Maupassant and Kate Chopin. Now let's take O. Henry's and Ernest
Hemingway's works as examples for further analysis.

O. HENRY
O. Henry's stories frequently have surprising endings. Thus, his stories are also
known for their witty narration. Most of his stories are set in his own time, the early
20th century. Many take place in New York City and deal for the most part with
ordinary people such as clerks, policemen and waitresses. O. Henry had an inimitable
hand for isolating some elements of society and describing them with an incredible
economy and grace of language.
"The Cop and the Anthem" in Unit 5 is about a New York City hobo named
Soapy, who set out to get arrested so that he could be a guest of the city jail instead
of sleeping out in the cold winter. Despite efforts at petty theft, vandalism, disorderly
conduct, "mashing" with a young prostitute, etc., Soapy failed to draw the attention
of the police. Disconsolate, he paused in front of a church, where an organ anthem
inspired him to clean up his life, and was ironically charged for loitering and
sentenced to three months in prison. The most important characteristic of this story
is its humor or "smiling with tears," which O. Henry shows throughout the whole
story with rich rhetorical devices. He expresses his unique humor through rhetorical
devices (e.g., hyperbole, simile, metaphor, personification, irony) to make the reader
think more deeply about the story. Here are some examples.
"Don't you figure out that I might have had something to do with it?" said Soapy, not

Soapy threw stones at the glass windows in a shop, and he thought this time he
would realize his aspiration to his dreamy island, so he didn't run away. Conversely,
he waited there anticipating to be arrested like someone who wished to have some
luck. The simile conveys Soapy's eagerness to be caught at this moment.

ERNEST HEMINGWAY
Hemingway's style is fundamentally shaped in reaction to his experience of
World War I. After World War I, he and other modernists lost faith in the central
institutions of Western civilization by reacting against the elaborate style of 19th
century writers and by creating a style in which meaning is established through
dialogue, action and silence-a fiction in which nothing crucial-or at least very
little-is stated explicitly. Hemingway called his style the "iceberg theory": The
facts float above the water; the supporting structure and symbolism operate out of
sight. The concept of the "iceberg theory" is sometimes referred to as the "theory
of omissioniạHemingway believed the writer could describe one thing through
an entirely different thing that occurs below the surface. His "iceberg theory of
omissioniằ_s the foundation on which he builds his stories. The syntax, which lacks
subordinating conjunctions, creates static sentences. The photographic "snapshot"
style creates a collage of images. Many types of internal punctuation (colons,
semicolons, dashes, parentheses) are omitted in favor of short declarative sentences.
The sentences build on each other, as events build to create a sense of the whole.
Multiple strands exist in one story; an 'embedded text bridges to a different angle.
He also used other cinematic techniques such as "cutting" quickly from one scene to
the next, or "splicing" a scene into another. Intentional omissions allow the reader to
fill the gap, as though responding to instructions from the author, and create three-
dimensional prose. Hemingway habitually used the word "and" in place of commas.
This use of polysyndeton may serve to convey immediacy. Hemingway's polysyndetic
sentence-or in later works his use of subordinate clauses-uses conjunctions to
juxtapose startling visions and images.
In "A Day's Wait,' Hemingway skillfully uses conversations between the father
and his son to illustrate the fateful misunderstanding between them. This fateful

be shocked when the father answered "It doesn't bother me."

ways that the author uses language. The author's word choice, sentence structure and
paragraphs all work together to establish mood, image and meaning in the text. Style
describes how the author describes events, objects and ideas, consequently influencing
how we interpret the facts that are presented in the text. Look at the following example

Wording and phrasing can tell us about emotions in the scene, the setting and

Each version tells us a lot about the situation, the speaker and the person being

sentence structure or paragraph arrangement can influence the style and tone of a
piece of writing.
• Word and style
The language used by the author can convey subtle messages about attitudes,
values and cultural assumptions. Every choice of word or expression allows for tiny
distinctions to be made. In Examples 1 and 2 on Page 168, for example, two extracts
were compared. They use different expressions to describe a young person: child and
kid. While each word describes a young person, the connotations carried by each
differ. Till the end of the 16th century, "kid" was a word that was only used to refer
to the offspring of a goat. It was only extended to the offspring of humans as slang
in 1590. Slowly and gradually, the word came to be accepted as an alternative to
human offspring. Therefore, the word "kid sometimes can demonstrate affection.
Comparatively, "child is a formal way to refer to a human being that is not an adult.
Words can be formal or informal, depending on the occasion and the audience. For
instance, if a father is talking to his eight-year-old son about forestry and said: "The
foliage in the woodland was being desiccated," it would be inappropriate. It should be
much better if he said "The trees in the forest are drying up." Words also convey subtle
messages about attitudes. When describing someone, one can say "He is confident,
proud, or egotistical." The word "confident" sends a positive message about this person
while the word egotistical indicates that this person is overconfident to the point of
being self-centered. It is important to use exact words in writing. Precise words can

• Sentence and style
Besides words, writers also create different styles through sentence manipulation.
A writer might use a lot of verbs, or use a lot of compound sentences, or use a lot of
clauses in his or her writing. A writer might use a lot of absolute phrases or use none.
He or she might use short sentences, long sentences, one-word paragraphs or five-
page paragraphs. Whatever choices he or she makes regarding word choice and how
words are arranged in phrases, sentences and paragraphs affect the writer's style. The
following are some examples of different styles realized through the skillful use of
sentence structure.

• Paragraph and style
Some writers also use paragraphs as a way to present their style. For instance,
Maupassants writing is very simple and economical. He does a lot with only a little bit of
192 Writing Critically 1
space. His control of timing and pacing is incredible. How does Maupassant do it? One trick
Maupassant uses is writing lots of really short paragraphs; this technique keeps the story
moving at a fast pace. The paragraphs are often little more than a single, simple sentence (the
sentences are usually short, too). The following passage (from "The Necklace") describes the
day after the Loisels discovered they had lost the necklace:
Her husband returned about seven o'clock. He had found nothing.
He went to police headquarters, to the newspaper offices to offer a reward; he went to
the cab companies-everywhere, in fact, whither he was urged by the least spark of hope.
She waited all day, in the same condition of mad fear before this terrible calamity.
Loisel returned at night with a hollow, pale face. He had discovered nothing.
This excerpt describes an entire day, with two characters and lots of scene changes,
encapsulated in just a few lines of text. Note that there is barely any description in this
passage, a fact highlighted by the distinct lack of adjectives, adverbs and descriptive
language. It just says what it needs to. And it reads like a charm. Maupassant knows
exactly what he needs to put in a passage to make it work, and uses no more.
When he does write longer paragraphs, Maupassant uses another notable
technique: He strings together sentences that begin with the same word and have the
same basic structure. For instance:
She came to know what heavy housework meant and the odious cares of the kitchen.
She washed the dishes, using her dainty fingers and rosy nails on greasy pots and pans
She washed the soiled linen, the shirts and the dishcloths, which she dried upon a line; she
carried the slops down to the street every morning and carried up the water, stopping for
breath at every landing. And dressed like a woman of the people, she went to the fruiterer,
the grocer, the butcher, a basket on her arm, bargaining, meeting with impertinence,
defending her miserable money, sou by sou.
If you think about it, starting every sentence with the sentence structure in bold
seems almost like an elementary and basic writing technique. Yet Maupassant makes
it work. When he mixes things up ever so slightly in that last sentence, by starting with
the "And dressed..." phrase before returning to "she went," it's just enough to keep
things interesting, and bring a sense of closure to the paragraph. All the repetition feels
ordered and neat. In Maupassant's hands, simplicity becomes elegance.

Part I: Learning the Skills
• Imagery as description
Description appears widely in all kinds of writing. It is especially indispensable in
narrative pieces. Description is defined as "picturing in words" in dictionaries which
200 Writing Critically 1
highlights the visual element as the basic feature. However, outstanding description
usually engages more than one of our five senses. We will achieve a far more striking
effect when we appeal to all five senses-sight, touch, smell, taste and sound.
Imagery can be used in just about any form of writing. Contemporary examples
of imagery include stories in newspapers and works of fiction. Imagery is also used in
songs, movies, television shows and everyday reports. This unit will analyze this powerful
descriptive device-imagery and the relevant figures of speech, which help build powerful
images. The selections in this unit are taken from poems as well as a variety of sources
such as songs or stories that are notable for their artistic handling of concrete language
and their ability to reach readers on various levels of sensual perception.
Take a look at Example 1 and see if you can figure out its use of imagery:
Example 1
On a starry winter night in Portugal
Where the ocean kissed the southern shore
There a dream I never thought would come to pass
Came and went like time spent through an hourglass
- "Portuguese Love" sung by Teena Marie
The lyrics above are taken from Teena Marie's hit love song entitled "Portuguese
Love"' Did you notice how descriptive it is? The line "the ocean kissed the southern shore"
can be easily associated with the sandbeach. "Hourglass," the device that measures the
passage of time from a few minutes up to an hour using sand also creates an image of time
passage associated with sand. In this excerpt alone, the imagery is increasingly apparent to
the reader. Even though this is a portion of the lyrics from a song, if you read it, you can
almost feel the sand of the beach beneath your feet.
Furthermore, you can see the similarity in the images created by Brueghel's
painting and Williams' poem. This painting presents the very moment of the tragedy,
when Icarus dropped into the water. His feet were struggling above the water, but his
efforts were in vain. It was the most tragic moment for the father, who witnessed his
son dying but could do nothing to save him. What is most shocking is how peaceful
and uninterested the world was. The farmer was busy ploughing; the ship went on
sailing; the warm sun and the tranquil sea did not notice the death of a young man.
Only his father in the air, stunned and helpless, was aware of the tragedy. This is the
way of the world the painter wants to indicate: No matter how much sorrow you
have, do not expect others to share it. You should swallow the pain and be tough. The
world keeps going on regardless of whatever you are suffering.
Responding to the painting, William Carlos Williams, a representative of
American imagists in the 20th century, wrote a poem with the same title as the
painting. The death of Icarus, the poet tells us "According to Brueghel, took place in
spring when the year was emerging in all its pageantry. The poem has no set rhyme
scheme or meter, an example of Williams' many free verse poems. It shares with the
painting the same theme, i.e., a feeling of insignificance: The tragic event of Icarus'

death was "quite unnoticed." The irony of the death of Icarus, who has always been
an emblem for the poet's upward flight that ends in tragedy, is that his death went
unnoticed in the spring-"a mere splash in the sea."
One factor contributing to this feeling is the stanza organization. Each stanza is
very short, usually containing a sentence or less, and includes many enjambments:
"a farmer was ploughing/his field/the whole pageantry" and "of the year was/awake
tingling/near." The considerably short length of each stanza creates a feeling of
unimportance. With no attempt at describing the scene in any depth, Williams just
gives the reader a superficial view of the scene. There are also some stanzas that
explicitly state the insignificance of Icarus' fall,ithe edge of the sea/concerned/with
itself," "unsignificantly/off the coast/there was' and "a splash quite unnoticed/this
was/Icarus drowningạiỊThe first of these stanzas relates back to the painting, where
one can see Icarus drowning at the edge of the sea. As the stanza reads, "the edge of
the sea/concerned/with itselfiẠỊthe idea that not even the ocean cares about Icarus
drowning fills the reader's mind. In the painting, the part that has Icarus drowning
is extremely small and tucked away in the corner, away from the eyes of the viewer.
Williams accentuates this unimportance by "unsignificantly/off the coast/there was"
and a splash quite unnoticed/this was/Icarus drowning.
• Types of imagery
Although most of the image-making words in any language appeal to sight
(visual), there are also images of sound (auditory), touch (tactile), taste (gustatory),
smell (olfactory) and movement (kinesthetic).
1. Visual imagery
Since, for most of us, sight is the primary sense we use to perceive the world, it
follows naturally that most writers use a lot of visual imagery. Visual imagery describes
how an object looks, and enables the reader to visualize the objects or actions.
Look at Example 2 and appreciate the strong visual images:
In our kitchen, he would bolt his orange juice (squeezed on one of those ribbed glass
sombreros and then poured off through a strainer) and grab a bite of toast (the toaster a
simple tin box, a kind of little hut with slit and slanted sides, that rested over a gas burner
and browned one side of the bread, in stripes, at a time), and then he would dash, so
hurriedly that his necktie flew back over his shoulder, down through our yard, past the
grapevines hung with buzzing Japanese-beetle traps, to the yellow brick building, with its
tall smokestack and wide playing fields, where he taught.

schoolteacher father. You could see that everything and every action is described in

"dash," "flew" vividly show that the father is in a hurry to go to work.

• Using imagery in your writing
Imagery, in a literary text, is a writer's use of vivid and descriptive language to
add depth to his or her work. Good descriptions are generally rich in imagery. The
reader can imagine actually seeing or hearing or touching the things described.
Imagery intensifies the impact of the writer's words as he or she shows us with his
or her words rather than just telling us. It appeals to human senses to deepen their
understanding of the work.
Good writers do not use imagery merely for decoration. They do not ask themselves,
"How can I dress up my subject so that it will seem fancier than it is?" Rather, they ask
themselves, "How can I make my subject appear to the reader exactly as it appears to
me?" Imagery helps them solve their problem, as it enables them to present their subject
as it is, that is, as it looks, smells, tastes, feels and sounds. Imagery is equally important to
the reader: It provides their imagination with something palpable to seize upon and helps
them understand the work by activating their senses.

2. Ideas and emotions through imagery
William Carlos Williams said that there are "no ideas but in things." For a good
writer creating good images, a thing can equal an idea.
Ideas may not be easily perceived and sometimes even cannot be defined: love,
hope, anger, pain, sorrow, and so on. Nothing is specifically about these words-their
meanings are ambiguous and leave a lot to interpret. Long strings of abstractions are
tiresome, and do not serve your writing well. The reader will place their associations
onto the abstraction and your intention may be lost. Writing is about precision, and
abstractions are anything but precise.
Therefore, if you are writing about some idea or concept, you need to show it
through images. Imagery explains abstractions in more perceptible and tangible
forms. This is a device by which the writer makes his or her meaning strong, clear
and certain. The more abstract your concept for the writing, the more precise your
imagery should be. Even if your writing relies heavily on ideas, you are obliged to
help your reader understand your writing. You are not the maker of puzzles. If your
reader is baffled, you have not done your job as a writer. One precise image is worth
pages of ideas.

Part III: Language Study
Imagery is the use of language to represent actions, feelings and other sensory
and extra-sensory experiences. Ezra Pound once described a poetic image as
something that captures an emotional and intellectual complex in an instant of time.
The words used to freeze an image are not a simple stand-in for an object; they
communicate a full human experience on an intellectual, sensual and emotional level.
Capturing a moment in time is what makes imagery in description poignant, and
the possibility of missing the experience gives the image power. Writers must freeze
the image as completely as possible so that something fleeting in reality, like eating a
piece of candy or seeing a shooting star, becomes a long-lasting experience that the
reader can re-live again and again.
Imagery could often be presented through the use of five senses and/or figurative
language.
• Using five senses
Imagery may be defined as the representation through language of a sensory
experience. It is important to sharpen your five senses (i.e., sight, touch, taste, smell
and sound), since they are the tools you use to create your images. Training the
senses is all about noticing. Descriptive language depends on the writer's ability to
observe and translate those observations into concrete language.

• Using figurative language
Figurative language, constantly used in imagery creation, particularly in poems,
says one thing while suggesting another, such as a metaphor or a simile. A poet could
simply state or say "I see a tree,' but it is possible to conjure up much more specific
images using techniques such as simile ("a tree like a spiky rocket"), metaphor ("a
green cloud riding a pole") or synecdoche ("bare, black branches")-each of these
suggests a different kind of tree. In this unit, we will take two types of figurative
language-simile and metaphor as examples to show how figurative language can
help build strong images.
1. Simile and imagery
Similes can be found everywhere in poems. When Lord Byron wants to describe
the savage attack of the Assyrian army in "The Destruction of Sennacherib," he
compares it to a wolf attacking a "fold of sheep:

Notice that Byron says the Assyrian was like "a wolf on the fold." Similes help
make an image more precise. You can feel the terror of the attack of the Assyrians in
Byron's writing.

2. Metaphor and imagery
A metaphor has two parts: the tenor, the main subject of the metaphor, and the
220 Writing Critically 1
vehicle, the thing that the tenor is being compared to. For instance, in the metaphor
"You are a shiny apple," "you' is the tenor, and the "shiny apple' is the vehicle. In
order to create a metaphor, the tenor and the vehicle must be dissimilar. A good
metaphor does not compare an apple to a plum, but an apple to something wholly
different, like a person one loves.
It has often been said that the heart of poetic language is the way it makes
comparisons, which seems to be strange and throws a new or even surprising light
on things or ideas. Poetry can bring to life inanimate things, like a city, a storm or
abstract ideas by using personification, which can make metaphors fresh and vivid.
Now read the following poem written by Emily Dickinson, a great poet in using
metaphors. What are the major metaphors in this poem? Find the tenors and the
vehicles. What was Dickinson saying about death or her knowledge of death? The
speaker only guessed ("surmised) that they were heading for eternity. Why did she
have to guess? She had experienced life, but what did she know about being dead? And
why didn't Death tell her? If eternity was their goal, could Immortality be a passenger?
Because I Could Not Stop for Death
Because I could not stop for Death-
He kindly stopped for me-
The Carriage held but just Ourselves—
And Immortality.
We slowly drove- He knew no haste
And I had put away
My labor and my leisure too,
For His Civility-
We passed the School, where Children strove
At Recess-in the Ring-
We passed the Fields of Gazing Grain-
We passed the Setting Sun-
Or rather-He passed Us-
The Dews drew quivering and chill-
For only Gossamer, my Gown-
My Tippet-only Tulle-
We paused before a House that seemed
A Swelling of the Ground-
The Roof was scarcely visible-
The Cornice-in the Ground-
Since then-'tis Centuries-and yet

Feels shorter than the Day
I first surmised the Horses Heads
Were toward Eternity-
In this poem, Death is personified as a carriage driver. The drive symbolizes
the speaker's passing life. She progressed from childhood (We passed the School'),
maturity (the "Gazing Grain" is ripe) and dying ("the Setting Sun") to her grave.
In the final stanza, the speaker had moved into death; the language in this stanza
becomes abstract while in the previous stanzas the imagery is concrete and specific.

Appendix 1
Narrative Essay Organization
A narrative is a story. When you write a narrative essay, you write about events in
detail. A narrative essay has an introduction that engages the reader's interest, a body
that gives details about the main event or action in the story, and a conclusion that
describes the outcome.
Introduction
• The hook gets the reader's attention.
• The middle sentences introduce an event (the action of the story) by providing
background information about the people, the place, and the time.
• The thesis statement prepares the reader for the action that follows.
Body Paragraphs
• The body paragraphs describe what happened in the story.
• They include details that bring the story to life.
• They often use time order to explain the event.
Conclusion
A conclusion describes the outcome of the event.
• It often ends with a comment by the writer about what the event showed or
taught.
(from Savage & Mayer, 2005, p. 58)

Appendix 2
The Writing Process
1. Brainstorming
Before you begin to write, gather information about the topic. Then, brainstorm
ideas and vocabulary related to the topic. Read your assignment carefully so that your
finished product will meet your instructor's expectations.
• Strategies: Read about the topic and discuss it with your classmates. Look at
pictures or diagrams to help you come up with ideas.
2. Creating an outline
Decide which ideas you will use in your essay. Cluster ideas into logical parts.
This may be in the form of a chart, a web, or a list of main ideas. Write an outline or
plan for your paper.
Strategies: Look at models that are similar to the writing that you want to do. Learn
ways to organize and sequence your ideas. Create a visual plan for your paper.
3. Writing a first draft
Expand your outline into a draft by rewriting your notes into full sentences. At
this stage, don't worry about mistakes. When you have finished, ask a classmate to
read your work and give you feedback.
• Strategies: Evaluate your outline as you write. Take out ideas that do not support
your argument; add clarification or examples. Check your work to make sure
your writing is clear and accomplishes the goals of the assignment.
4. Editing
Now apply your knowledge of grammar and mechanics, and correct any
mistakes that you notice. Review the feedback you received from your classmates.
• Strategies: Separate yourself from the ideas so that you can focus on clarity at the
sentence level. If possible, put your paper aside for a few hours before you edit.
Read your essay sentence by sentence. (Some writers read a paper backwards so
as not to be distracted by content.)
5. Writing a final draft and submitting your work
Rewrite your drafts so that it looks neat and has all the features of a finished
college paper. Some writers type their paper; others write by hand.
• Strategies: Make sure your paper has the correct format. Make sure your name
and the data are on the paper, and that there is a title.
(from Savage & Mayer, 2005, p. 160)
Appendix 3
Suggestions on Narrative Writing
(Beginnings, Endings, Being Specific,
Showing Instead of Telling)
In the pieces that follow, three professional writers give their ideas on story
beginnings and endings, being specific, and the importance of showing instead of
telling. We think you will find these hints useful in improving your writing.
Beginnings
(Christina Baldwin)
I tell writing students that the beginning of a story is like the threshold of a
doorway. You want the reader to feel confident enough in the imagined world so that
he/she will step into the story's reality without hesitating.
Endings
(Elizabeth Cowan)
Make the Most of Your Conclusion
Like the introduction, the conclusion must be "concocted." It is not organically
contained in the thesis as the middle of an essay is, so it has to come entirely out of
your head.
As with introductions, many writers fail to make the most of conclusions. Yet
your paper fizzles out at the end, the reader may forget what you said the minute he
finishes reading it. Having come this far, you should want to make sure your reader
doesn't end with a "Ho hum! So what?" So make the most of your conclusion.
Essay Conclusion
The ending of your paper ought to do three things:
1. Remind your readers of what you have said.
2. Give your readers at least one new thing to think about.
3. Provide a gentle completing of the paper so that your readers are not left
hanging in the air.
Be Specific
(Natalie Goldberg)
Be specific. Don't say "fruit." Tell what kind of fruit-"It is a pomegranate." Give
things the dignity of their names. Just as with human beings, it is rude to say, "Hey,
228 Writing Critically 1
girl, get in line." That "girl" has a name. (As a matter of fact, if she's at least twenty
years old, she's a woman, not a girl' at all.) Things, too, have names. It is much better
to say the geranium in the window" than "the flower in the window." "Geranium"-
that one word gives us a much more specific picture. It penetrates more deeply into
the beingness of that flower. It immediately gives us the scene by the window-red
petals, green circular leaves, all straining toward sunlight.
About ten years ago I decided I had to learn the names of plants and flowers in
my environment. I bought a book on them and walked down the tree-lined streets
of Boulder, examining leaf, bark, and seed, trying to match them up with their
descriptions and names in the book: Maple, elm, oak, locust. I usually tried to cheat
by asking people working in their yards the names of the flowers and trees growing
there. I was amazed how few people had any idea of the names of the live beings
inhabiting their little plot of land.
When we know the name of something, it brings us closer to the ground. It takes
the blur out of our mind; it connects us to the earth. If I walk down the street and see
"dogwood," "forsythia, I feel more friendly toward the environment. I am noticing
what is around me and can name it. It makes me more awake.
If you read the poems of William Carlos Williams, you will see how specific he
is about plants, trees, flowers-chicory, daisy, locust, poplar, quince, primrose, black-
eyed susan, lilacs-each has its own integrity. Williams says, "Write what's in front of
your nose." It's good for us to know what is in front of our nose. Not just "daisy, but
how the flower in the season we are looking at it-"The dayseye hugging the earth/in
August... brownedged,/green and pointed scales/armor his yellowịằ_Continue to hone
your awareness: to the name, to the month, to the day, and finally to the moment.
Williams also says: "No ideas but in things." Study what is "in front of your nose."
By saying "geranium" instead of "flower," you are penetrating more deeply into the
present and being there. The closer we can get to what's in front of our nose, the more
it can teach us everything. "To see a World in a Grain of Sand and a Heaven in a Wild
Flower.iẠạ
In writing groups and classes too, it is good to quickly learn the names of all
the other group members. It helps to ground you in the group and make you more
attentive to each other's work.
Learn the names of everything: birds, cheese, tractors, cars, buildings. A writer
is all at once everything-an architect, French cook, farmer-and at the same time, a
writer is none of these things.
Don't Tell, but Show
(Natalie Goldberg)
There is an old adage in writing "Don't tell, but show? What does this actually
mean? It means don't tell us about anger (or any of those big words like honesty,
truth, hate, love, sorrow, life, justice, etc.); show us what made you angry. We will
read it and feel angry. Don't tell readers what to feel. Show them the situation, and
that feeling will awaken in them.
Writing is not psychology. We do not talk "about" feelings. Instead the writer
feels and through her words awakens those feelings in the reader. The writer takes
the reader's hand and guides him through the valley of sorrow and joy without ever
having to mention those words.
When you are present at the birth of a child you may find yourself weeping and
singing. Describe what you see: the mother's face, the rush of energy when the baby
finally enters the world after many attempts, the husband breathing with his wife,
applying a wet washcloth to her forehead. The reader will understand without your
ever trying to discuss the nature of life.
When you write, stay in direct connection with the senses and what you are
writing about. If you are writing from first thoughts-the way your mind first flashes
on something before second and third thoughts take over and comment, criticize,
and evaluate-you won't have to worry. First thoughts are the mind reflecting
experiences-as close as a human being can get in words to the sunset, the birth, the
bobby pin, the crocus. We can't always stay with first thoughts, but it is good to know
about them. They can easily teach us how to step out of the way and use words like a
mirror to reflect the pictures.
As soon as I hear the word about in someone's writing, it is an automatic alarm.
"This story is about life." Skip that line and go willy-nilly right into the life in your
writing. Naturally, when we do practice writing in our notebooks, we might write
a general line: "I want to write about my grandmother" or "This is a story about
success." That's fine. Don't castigate yourself for writing it; don't get critical and mix
up the creator and editor. Simply write it, note it, and drop to a deeper level and enter
the story and take us into it.
Some general statements are sometimes very appropriate. Just make sure to back
each one with a concrete picture. Even if you are writing an essay, it makes the work
so much more lively. Oh, if only Kant or Descartes had followed these instructions,
"I think, therefore I am"-I think about bubble gum, horse racing, barbecue, and
the stock market; therefore, I know I exist in America in the twentieth century. Go
ahead, take Kant's Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics and get it to show what he
is telling. We should all be a lot happier.
Several years ago I wrote down a story that someone had told me. My friends
said it was boring. I couldn't understand their reaction; I loved the story. What I
realize now is that I wrote "about" the story, secondhand. I didn't enter it and make
friends with it. I was outside it; therefore, I couldn't take anyone else into it. This does
not mean you can't write about something you did not actually experience firsthand;
only make sure that you breathe life into it. Otherwise it is two times removed and
you are not present.
(from Withrow, Brookes, & Cummings, 1996, p. 240-244)

Appendix 4
After Writing
Each After Writing section has two types of activities: sharing your writing and
giving feedback (or responding) to your classmates' writing, and reflecting on how
you wrote (your writing process).
You will be asked to share your writing with your classmates, either by exchanging
papers and reading silently or by reading your piece aloud. After you read or listen to your
classmates' writing, you will be asked to give a response or feedback based on questions
or guidelines provided. Sometimes this is done in a group, sometimes with a partner, and
occasionally you may be asked to give yourself feedback on your own writing.
The questions in the After Writing sections are about things any reader or
listener can respond to concerning a piece of writing. They are not technical. That is,
you are not expected to give feedback as an editor or teacher. You don't have to give
suggestions for revision or make corrections. Simply be yourself as an active reader
or listener, and say something to the writer. Use the questions as guidelines.
Here are a few examples of the kinds of questions you will be asked to respond to
in After Writing:
What do you like about the composition?
What do you understand about it?
What details stand out for you, the reader?
What point does this piece make?
How could this piece of writing be improved?
What examples does the writer include?
Do the examples illustrate the writer's point?
How does the writer develop the point (idea)?
Some of the terms used in these After Writing questions may not be familiar to
you at first. If you don't understand certain terms, discuss them with your instructor
and classmates. Try to use words as you think they should be used. They will become
clearer as you go along. Remember, there are no right or wrong answers.
A few terms used frequently in the After Writing questions are defined here
briefly. The reading passages throughout the book contain many examples of each
term. If you discuss these terms with your instructor and classmates, look back at
some of the readings for examples.
Point: central idea; what the writing trying to say; the message; the lesson; may
be implied or stated explicitly.
Example: a story, an experience, or other specifics used to illustrate a point.
Detail: a bit of added information, often sensory (visual, auditory, related to
touch or feeling, etc.)
Development: how the writer starts, builds, and concludes an idea or a point
throughout a piece of writing.
(from Withrow, Brookes, & Cummings, 1996, p. 245-246)
